candidates.title: Structural basis for coupled DNA replication and uracil repair by a family of DNA polymerases from phages with T-modified genomes
candidates.authors: Missoury S, Lucas-Staat S, Sieskind R, Delarue M.
candidates.abstract: AbstractReplicative DNA polymerases (DNAPs) play a critical role in genome duplication, ensuring the accurate transmission of genetic information in all domains of life. DNAPs are also essential for DNA viruses, as well as bacteriophages, where a uracil-DNA glycosylase (UDG) is often encoded in trans or is present in the DNAP gene. Here, we identify a new group of A-family DNAPs in phages that are fused to an active UDG domain and contain other large insertions. Several members of this subfamily, including phages SP-15 and YerA41, are known to be hypermodified on their thymidine base through glycosylation of a linker attached to the C5 position of thymine. We determined the atomic cryo-EM structures for two of its members in various active functional and conformational states, from YerA41 and phiLo phages. The structures reveal how these large DNAPs function as replicative DNAPs, and how they can recognize dU bases ahead of the replication fork through their UDG domain, generating abasic sites that are preferentially bypassed through dA incorporation. Such dU errors would need to be eliminated to preserve phage genome integrity. Additionally, we report the co-occurrence of both an X-family DNAP and a DNA ligase in the corresponding phage genomes and show that both enzymes can execute the final steps of base excision repair most probably on-the-fly during replication, revealing a DNA-replication-coupled repair process. The structures of these large polymerases can serve as a model of other large platform DNAPs that can recruit additional enzymatic activities necessary for phage or virus survival.

candidates.title: Structure Basis for Chloride Recognition and Transport by Human Kidney Brain Anion Transporter (KBAT)
candidates.authors: Wang Y, Xie T, Wu S, Wang A, Cheng W, Huang J, Yan R, Chi X.
candidates.abstract: AbstractSLC26A11, also known as the kidney and brain anion transporter (KBAT), mediates the transport of multiple anionic substrates across the plasma membrane. It is highly enriched in cerebellar Purkinje cells, where loss of KBAT results in hyperpolarized membrane potentials and increased intrinsic firing frequency, correlating with locomotor dysfunction. Despite its physiological significance, the molecular basis of substrate recognition and transport by KBAT remains elusive. Here, we present the structure of full-length human KBAT in an inward-facing conformation with chloride ions (Cl−) bound. Sequence analysis of the substrate-binding pockets uncovers the important residue E320 in KBAT. Protonation of E320 abolishes its interaction with S363 and correlates with Cl− binding in the canonical substrate pocket, as substantiated by molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. Quantitative MD contact analysis delineates the rearrangements of residue interactions underlying the alternative access transport, consistent with an elevator-like transport mechanism. The cross-arranged transmembrane helices of the Gate and Core domains require minimal conformational rearrangement to achieve alternating access to the membrane. Collectively, our study provides a critical foundation for comprehensively understanding the recognition and transport mechanisms of human KBAT, with potential implications for developing therapies for neuronal swelling.Keywords: kidney brain anion transporter (KBAT), protonation-dependent Cl− recruitment, transport conformational switch

candidates.title: 6PPD-Quinone Induces Anxiety-like Behavior in Mice: A Potential Mechanism Shared Across PPD-Quinones
candidates.authors: Xu S, Gao L, Yu Y, Kang Y, Chen X, Wang S, Ruan Z.
candidates.abstract: AbstractThe increasing occurrence of anxiety disorders caused by emerging environmental toxicants has become a significant global health concern. While recent evidence indicates that 6PPD-Q can induce anxiety-like behavior, the specific mechanisms connecting 6PPD-Q to anxiety-like behavior are still largely unknown. This gap in understanding restricts our knowledge of their neurotoxic potential and complicates the development of targeted treatment strategies. Here, adverse effects, including neuronal degeneration, synaptic dysfunction, and impaired GABAergic signaling in the amygdala, were observed in mice exhibiting anxiety-like behavior following 6PPD-Q exposure. Integrated network toxicology and transcriptomic analysis revealed that inhibition of the cAMP signaling pathway was associated with PPD-Q-related anxiety-like behavior, and adenosine receptors, particularly ADORA2A, as potential targets of 6PPD-Q. Specifically, molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulations suggested that 6PPD-Q may stably interact with the orthosteric ligand-binding pocket of ADORA2A, potentially interfering with receptor activation. Importantly, the predicted interaction with ADORA2A may represent a potentially shared neurotoxicological feature among PPD-Qs, consistent with the computationally predicted interaction profiles across PPD-Qs. Moreover, pharmacological activation of ADORA2A with the selective agonist significantly alleviated the 6PPD-Q-induced neurobehavioral deficits in mice. Collectively, our research provides evidence supporting the involvement of ADORA2A and the cAMP-related signaling pathway in 6PPD-Q-induced anxiety-like behavior, providing a timely foundation for preventing neuropsychiatric disorders associated with PPD-Q exposure.Keywords: 6PPD-Q, PPD-Qs, anxiety-like behavior, cAMP signaling, ADORA2A

candidates.title: A Cell-Based ELISA for High-Throughput Screening of Inhibitors Blocking Influenza Virus Attachment to the Subtype-Independent α2,6-Sialic Acid Receptor
candidates.abstract: AbstractRising drug resistance underscores the urgent need for novel anti-influenza strategies. Targeting the hemagglutinin (HA)–sialic acid receptor interaction offers a promising broad-spectrum approach, yet progress is impeded by the lack of screening models that report the receptor-recognition step in a subtype-independent manner. Herein, we established a robust cell-based ELISA platform for high-throughput screening (HTS) that operates on the subtype-independent receptor-recognition step. The model utilizes ST6GAL1-overexpressing MDCK cells to enrich human-type α2,6-sialic acid receptors and employs horseradish peroxidase (HRP)-conjugated Sambucus nigra lectin (SNA) as a functional, though not structural, surrogate for the receptor-recognition step, yielding a high Z’ factor of 0.78. Given that SNA is a lectin rather than HA, the assay cannot by itself distinguish HA-specific blockade from membrane-mediated or virucidal effects. Orthogonal validation is therefore required for every hit. Screening a library of 2600 compounds identified two hits, Hypericin and protoporphyrin IX (PPIX), which effectively blocked SNA–receptor recognition with IC50 values of 18.39 ± 6.23 μM and 9.77 ± 3.05 μM, respectively. An orthogonal flow cytometry assay with FITC-conjugated SNA reproduced this inhibition on intact cells in a dose-dependent manner (IC50 = 17.68 ± 9.54 μM for Hypericin and 25.31 ± 19.47 μM for PPIX), confirming that the inhibition is not an artifact of the colorimetric readout. Hemagglutination inhibition (HA) assays with distinct pre-incubation strategies indicated that both compounds act on the viral particle rather than on the host receptor. Surface plasmon resonance (SPR) and molecular docking studies further indicated direct, dose-dependent but low-affinity binding to HA proteins. Notably, cytopathic effect (CPE) assays demonstrated their potent antiviral efficacy across H1N1 and H3N2 subtypes, with PPIX exhibiting exceptionally potent activity against H3N2 (EC50 = 0.50 ± 0.17 μM). Taken together, these data identify Hypericin and PPIX as viral-side attachment inhibitors with weak HA binding and multimodal antiviral activity. Because neither a virucidal nor a fusion-blocking control was included, the relative contribution of HA engagement to their overall antiviral effect remains to be established. In conclusion, this BSL-1-compatible ELISA platform, which probes the subtype-independent receptor-recognition step, provides an efficient tool for discovering broad-spectrum influenza entry inhibitors, and the identified hits offer novel pharmacological scaffolds for further structural optimization.Keywords: influenza viruses; high-throughput screening model; entry inhibitors; hemagglutinin; Sambucus nigra agglutinin (SNA); α-2,6-sialic acid; subtype-independent receptor recognition

candidates.title: A Cluster-Guided Screening Framework for Prioritizing Natural Product Candidates Against HIV-1 from the KNApSAcK Database
candidates.authors: Alqaaf M, Mamun M, Nasution A, Islam A, Supriyanti R, Ono N, Kanaya S, Altaf-Ul-Amin M.
candidates.abstract: AbstractBackground: Plant-derived natural products are a productive antiviral scaffold source, yet secondary metabolite libraries remain underexplored against HIV-1 amid extensive target-structure redundancy. This study presents a cluster-guided framework for HIV-1 inhibitor prioritization from the KNApSAcK database. Methods: A total of 64,166 SMs were converted to SMILES and queried against BindingDB to identify reported HIV-1 integrase, protease, and reverse-transcriptase associations. A total of 295 HIV-1 protein sequences were aligned and partitioned using DPClusSBO; representative structures (6VDK, 1MUI, 6ELI) per cluster were docked against cluster-mapped SMs using SMINA. Prioritized SMs were evaluated with SwissADME and benchmarked against ChEMBL HIV-1 inhibitors. Results: Clustering resolved three non-overlapping groups (integrase, n = 135; protease, n = 117; reverse transcriptase, n = 42), mapping 285, 124, and 410 SMs, respectively. Predicted docking scores ranged from −18.91 to −4.72 kcal/mol (integrase), −26.54 to −7.87 kcal/mol (protease), and −26.83 to −4.59 kcal/mol (reverse transcriptase). ADME-prioritized reverse-transcriptase compounds scored more favorably than the matched NNRTI reference set (p < 0.001), requiring experimental confirmation of binding affinity. DUD-E enrichment validation showed strong discriminative validity for integrase and protease (ROC-AUC 0.85, 0.78) but not reverse transcriptase (ROC-AUC 0.53), consistent with weaker pose reproduction for the latter. Conclusions: The framework reduced target redundancy and computationally prioritized natural product candidates for HIV-1 as hypothesis-generating predictions requiring experimental validation.Keywords: HIV-1, natural products, secondary metabolites, KNApSAcK, virtual screening, molecular docking, sequence-based clustering, ADME prediction

candidates.title: A Dipeptide Module Substitution-Based Strategy for the Modification and Evaluation of ACE Inhibitory Peptides
candidates.authors: Liang Q, Wang S, Sun N, Zhu C, Liu Z, Mou H.
candidates.abstract: Food-derived angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitory peptide LYPVK exhibits promising potential for application as an important ingredient with a potential antihypertensive effect in functional foods. However, the structure–activity relationship and the rational design strategy for peptide modification remain insufficiently understood. To address this, dipeptide module substitution was employed to modify and investigate the mechanism of this food-derived ACE inhibitory peptide, providing an insight into the structure–activity relationship. Through integration of molecular docking and activity verification, LY and YP within LYPVK were identified as potential low- and high-activity fragments, respectively. Meanwhile, EY and SY were screened as high-contribution ones, resulting in the generation of EYPVK and SYPVK, which exhibited 13.5% and 25.1% higher ACE inhibitory activity, respectively, compared with the original peptide LYPVK. The enhanced activity may be attributed to increased hydrogen bonds and hydrophobic interactions with ACE and the strengthening of Tyr-mediated binding by Glu or Ser residues in the peptide sequences. Cellular assays showed altered nitric oxide (NO) and endothelin-1 (ET-1) levels, suggesting their potential function at the endothelial cell level. Additionally, SYPVK may regulate multiple targets and pathways for its function, as indicated by the network pharmacology and real-time fluorescence quantitative PCR analysis. These findings demonstrate that dipeptide module substitution is a viable approach for peptide optimization, highlighting the potential module effects in the design of functional peptides.

candidates.title: A Pathway-Driven Computational Drug Discovery Framework Integrating Machine Learning and Virtual Screening for Identification of Anti-Rheumatoid Arthritis Natural Small Molecules
candidates.authors: Sun J, Wang Y, Ye H, Chen J, Chen Y, Yao G.
candidates.abstract: Objective: This study aimed to establish a pathway-driven computational drug discovery framework integrating machine learning, target prioritization, virtual screening, molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, and in vitro evaluation to identify natural small molecules with potential anti-rheumatoid arthritis (RA) activity. Methods: Sixteen RA-related Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) datasets were included, with 15 cohorts used for model development and one reserved for independent external validation. Pathway features quantified by gene set variation analysis (GSVA) were subjected to cohort-aware feature selection using a leave-one-dataset-out framework across seven machine-learning algorithms. Predictive modeling and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analysis were subsequently performed, followed by random-effects meta-analysis (REMA) and network analysis for candidate-target prioritization. Natural compounds were screened by molecular docking and further evaluated using ligand efficiency, multiple scoring approaches, explicit-membrane MD simulations, and a TNF-α-induced MH7A inflammatory model. Results: Ten stable RA-associated pathways were identified. The final CAT+ET model achieved ROC-AUCs of 0.783 (95% CI, 0.731–0.836) and 0.610 (95% CI, 0.496–0.720) in the internal and independent external validation sets, respectively, indicating limited cross-cohort generalizability. SHAP and cross-cohort analyses supported Complement and coagulation cascades for downstream investigation, and integrated expression and network evidence prioritized C3AR1 as a candidate target. Virtual screening identified four candidate natural compounds (SM1–SM4). Ligand-size analysis, ligand efficiency, multiple scoring approaches, and explicit-membrane MD simulations provided complementary structural and energetic assessments of these candidates. Among them, SM1 showed comparatively favorable computational characteristics and a relatively consistent reduction in the inflammatory markers IL6 and MMP3 in TNF-α-stimulated MH7A cells, accompanied by changes in C3AR1 expression. These convergent computational and experimental findings supported the prioritization of SM1 for further investigation. Conclusions: This study established a pathway-driven framework linking cross-cohort pathway identification with candidate-target prioritization and natural-product screening in RA. Complement and coagulation cascades and C3AR1 were prioritized for downstream investigation, while integrated computational and experimental evidence identified SM1 as a candidate with promising anti-inflammatory potential. Although direct compound–C3AR1 engagement and its functional involvement require further validation, the present study provides a systematic and extensible strategy for translating robust RA-associated pathway signals into candidate targets and natural compounds, offering a valuable foundation for subsequent natural-product drug discovery in RA.

candidates.title: Actions of Pharmaceutical Lactones and Lactams on the Enzymes with Lactonase Activity: In Silico Prediction and In Vitro Study
candidates.abstract: Pharmaceutical pollutants that contain lactone or lactam rings in their structure are frequently detected in wastewater. Enzymes with lactonase activity, synthesized by the microorganisms in aerobic activated sludge, are expected to be able to participate in the hydrolysis of these pharmaceutical pollutants, but the actual activity of many lactonases towards such compounds remains poorly characterized. In this work, a systematic molecular docking study of 12 enzymes and 39 pharmaceutical pollutants (β-lactam antibiotics, macrolides, coumarins, statins) was undertaken. The binding affinity, active-site occupancy, total enzyme surface occupancy and geometric characteristics of the molecules (the distance from the catalytic nucleophile to the carbonyl carbon of the lactone ring, and the attack angle formed between the nucleophilic atom of the enzyme and the C–N/C–O bond of the substrate) were evaluated in silico for a set of hydrolases displaying lactonase activity (AidC, AaL, hexahistidine-tagged organophosphate hydrolase (His6-OPH), etc.) and metallo-β-lactamases (MβLs) (NDM-1, MIM-1, SAM-1). Lactamases exhibited favorable intermolecular interaction geometry for the majority of β-lactams. No enzyme was found that satisfied the geometric criteria corresponding to the biodegradation of macrolides. With coumarins, only Paraoxonase PON2 provided an optimal geometry of biocatalysis; however, this enzyme is absent from activated sludge but may be of interest for in vivo applications. For several statins widely used in practice, combinations with enzymes having virtually ideal geometry for biocatalysis were identified: AidC/rosuvastatin lactone, AaL/lovastatin, His6-OPH/mevastatin, and PON2/simvastatin. For the first time, several pharmaceutical lactones were identified in silico and confirmed in vitro as inhibitors of MβL and His6-OPH. Competitive inhibition of NDM-1 by lactone-containing signaling molecules of Gram-negative bacteria present in activated sludge was revealed for the first time both in silico and in vitro. The obtained results‘ may be taken into account when implementing monitoring of biological stages at water treatment stations and improve the efficiency of water purification. The revealed characteristics of MβL inhibition by macrolides may be taken into account as one of possible explanations for the effective application of β-lactams in combinations with macrolides known from multiple paratactical investigations.

candidates.title: Analysis of Ligation Activity in Miniaturized L1 Ligase Ribozyme Variants Down to 49 nt and in Split Ribozyme Forms
candidates.authors: Nitta Y, Kato M, Takagi Y, Saga Y, Ando T, Mutsuro-Aoki H, Tamura K.
candidates.abstract: Identifying the smallest active unit capable of ligating RNA in the absence of proteins is important to elucidate ribozyme evolution. Here, we aimed to construct an evolutionary model of the L1 ligase ribozyme. The miniaturized L1 ligase ribozyme (L1X6c2) consists of three stems: Stems A, B, and C. Mutants with shortened stems B and C were used to examine whether ligation occurred. In the mutant where both stems were simultaneously shortened, no ligation products were observed. We also constructed mutants with nucleotide deletions, measured their ligation-product signals after 24 h, and identified the structures crucial for ligation. A split mutant, formed by cleaving L1X6c2 at stem B, showed a ligation-product signal after 24 h close to that of L1X6c2, whereas another split mutant, formed by cleaving L1X6c2 at stem C, exhibited decreased activity. Although non-Watson–Crick base pairs near the ligation site did not affect ligation, the presence of G1 was important for ligation. Mutational analysis suggested that strong interactions between G1 and A51 in the G1–A51–U38 base triple are responsible for the base specificity of A51. Moreover, consecutive base pairs on each stem subtly contribute to the stability of the ribozyme folded into a compact structure to create a catalytic pocket.

candidates.title: Anthocyanin-Rich Morus alba L. Fruit Extract Phytosome Protects Neuronal Cells Against Oxidative Stress-Induced Cytotoxicity
candidates.authors: Khongrum J, Palachai N.
candidates.abstract: This study investigated the neuroprotective potential of an anthocyanin-rich Morus alba L. fruit extract phytosome (MAP) against hydrogen peroxide (H2O2)-induced oxidative stress and cellular injury in SH-SY5Y cells. Cells were treated with the MAP before and during H2O2 exposure. Cell viability and cytotoxicity were assessed using MTT and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) assays, respectively. Intracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS) production and malondialdehyde (MDA) accumulation were measured to evaluate oxidative stress, while antioxidant status was determined by assessing the activities of superoxide dismutase (SOD), catalase (CAT), and glutathione peroxidase (GSH-Px). Inflammatory responses were evaluated through the expression of tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) and nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB). Apoptosis-related proteins, including B-cell lymphoma 2 (Bcl-2) and Bcl-2-associated X protein (Bax), were also analyzed. Histone deacetylase (HDAC)/sirtuin 1 (SIRT1)-related responses were evaluated by determining HDAC activity and SIRT1 expression. The MAP treatment significantly improved cell viability and reduced LDH release following H2O2 exposure. These effects were accompanied by a significant reduction in HDAC activity and an increase in SIRT1 expression, which coincided with decreased ROS generation and lipid peroxidation, enhanced endogenous antioxidant defenses, attenuated expression of inflammatory mediators, and modulation of apoptosis-related signaling pathways. Collectively, these findings suggest that modulation of HDAC activity and SIRT1 expression may contribute to the protective activity of MAP, accompanied by the attenuation of oxidative stress, inflammation, and apoptosis-related responses. Further studies in animal models and humans are warranted to validate the neuroprotective potential of MAP and assess its potential as a food-derived bioactive ingredient.

candidates.title: Antibacterial and Multi-Target Immunomodulatory Mechanisms of Marine Nocardia rhizosphereae Metabolites: Experimental and Network Pharmacology
candidates.authors: Maliehe T, Shekwa W, Pooe O, Masoko P.
candidates.abstract: AbstractThe constant increase in multidrug resistance has necessitated bioprospecting of marine actinomycetes for potent antibacterial and immunomodulatory activities. The aim of this study was to investigate the antibacterial and potential host-immunomodulatory mechanisms of secondary metabolites from marine Nocardia rhizosphereae. The extract of N. rhizosphereae was characterised using Gas Chromatography–Mass Spectrometry (GC-MS), and its minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) was determined by a microdilution assay. Network pharmacology analysis, Gene Ontology (GO) and Kyoto Encyclopaedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathway enrichment analyses were performed using ShinyGO to elucidate potential host-immunomodulatory mechanisms against bacterial infections. Molecular docking was done using Attracting Cavities on SwissDock. GC–MS spectra revealed 33 compounds, of which 11, including 2-pentanone, 4-amino-4-methyl (50.11%) and 2-hexanol, 2-methyl (25.4%), were reported in extracts with antibacterial activities. The extract exhibited MIC values ranging from 19.55 to 312.5 µg/mL. Key hub targets included ESR1, HSP90AA1 and PPARG. GO enrichment revealed 457 molecular functions, while KEGG analysis illustrated 156 pathways. The best docking poses ranged between –4.99 and −8.69 kcal/mol. In conclusion, the metabolites showed potential antibacterial activity through disruption of bacterial cell-envelope integrity and potential modulation of multiple host-associated molecular targets and signalling pathways.Keywords: Nocardia rhizosphereae, antibacterial activity, antibacterial mechanism, network pharmacology, molecular docking

candidates.title: Binding of a Novel 11β-Hydroxysteroid to the Apelin Receptor (APLNR) and Its Possible Role in Regulating Skeletal Muscle Health in Mice
candidates.authors: González-Pérez M, Gómez-Márquez C, Ortiz-Flores M, Godínez-Victoria M, Nájera N, Ceballos G.
candidates.abstract: Several molecules have been investigated for their potential to improve muscle health in models of muscle damage simulating sarcopenia, injury, or aging. Some small molecules induced beneficial effects on skeletal muscle by stimulating the apelin receptor (APLNR). This receptor has emerged as a promising pharmacological target for modulating muscle homeostasis. Using an in silico approach, we recently identified 11β-hydroxypregnenolone (11β-OHP5) as a potential skeletal muscle (SKM) modulator. We hypothesized that 11β-OHP5 interacts with and activates APLNR. This study employed several research approaches: (1) in silico molecular docking and molecular dynamics to explore the feasibility of 11β-OHP5 interacting with APLNR; (2) in vitro activation analysis to APLNR; (3) in vitro analysis C2C12 myoblast differentiation; (4) analysis of the molecule’s presence in mouse skeletal muscle and its differential presence between young and older mice. The results show that 11β-OHP5, acting through APLNR, positively affects myoblast differentiation and may participate in the exercise-induced benefits in aging mice. We show that 11β-OHP5 interacts with APLNR, induces myogenic responses, is found in SKM; its concentration decreases with age, and exercise restores it. More work is necessary to understand the physiology of this possible endogenous molecule.

candidates.title: Biogenic Selenium Nanoparticle-Based Nanocomposite Hydrogel for Dual Delivery of Curcumin and Simvastatin for Topical Wound Healing Applications
candidates.authors: Kasem N, Sarhan H, Mostafa M, Hofny H, Abouzed D, Elsayed M, Mostafa M.
candidates.abstract: Background: Chronic and ischemic wounds are dysregulated, causing inflammation, oxidative stress, and bacterial colonization. This work developed a bionanocomposite hydrogel using biogenic selenium nanoparticles (SeNPs) to encapsulate and topically distribute two weakly water-soluble medicines, curcumin (Curc) and simvastatin (SMV), to improve wound healing. Methods: Green production of biogenic SeNPs utilizing Psidium guajava (guava) leaf extract. Based on entrapment efficiency (%EE; E1) and cumulative drug release after 2 and 8 h (E2) and (E3), a two-factor, three-level Box–Behnken design selected the SeNP-to-drug weight ratio (C1) and ethanol concentration (C2). The selected nanoconstruct was integrated into a 2% w/v Carbopol 934 hydrogel and characterized by UV-vis, FTIR, SEM, and DLS. In a 14-day full-thickness excisional wound model in Wistar rats, wound contraction, tissue remodeling, inflammatory responses, and healing kinetics were examined to determine its therapeutic efficiency. Results: Formulation F9 had the highest overall attractiveness (0.998) and %EE values of 94.71% for SMV and 93.92% for Curc. DLS showed a hydrodynamic particle size of 177.7 nm and PDI of 0.41. Both medications were successfully incorporated without chemical incompatibility based on FTIR analysis. The selected nanogel maintained a skin-friendly pH of 6.2 ± 0.1 and sustained biphasic drug release. In vivo, the half-dose nanogel showed an enhanced wound-healing response, accelerating wound contraction and achieving complete epithelialization in 14 ± 1.06 days (p < 0.05) compared to 22 ± 2.5 days for the sham control, corresponding to a 36% reduction in healing time. Histopathology showed epidermal thickness restoration and well-organized collagen deposition. In addition, therapy dramatically decreased the proinflammatory biomarkers IL-1β, MMP-9, and COX-2 and increased IL-10 levels without causing tissue discomfort. Conclusions: The biogenic SeNP-based nanogel delivers Curc and SMV locally with prolonged drug release and anti-inflammatory and tissue-remodeling effects. The half-dose combination accelerated wound healing while retaining tissue compatibility, suggesting this green nanocomposite hydrogel could be a promising topical method for advanced cutaneous wound therapy.

candidates.title: Biological Effects of Umbelliferone in MCF-7 Breast Cancer Cells: Integrated In Vitro and Computational Analyses
candidates.abstract: AbstractBackground/Objectives: Breast cancer remains a leading cause of cancer-related mortality among women, highlighting the need for further investigation of bioactive compounds with selective effects on cancer cells. This study evaluated the biological effects of the natural coumarin derivative umbelliferone in MCF-7 breast cancer cells using integrated in silico and in vitro approaches. Methods: Molecular docking predicted interactions with AKT1, mTOR, PI3Kα, and Caspase-7, while molecular dynamics simulations and MM/PBSA calculations provided further information on interactions with AKT1 and mTOR. Results: Umbelliferone reduced MCF-7 cell viability in a concentration-dependent manner, with an IC50 of 492 µM after 24 h, whereas 50% viability was not reached in BJ normal fibroblasts up to 1400 µM, corresponding to an IC50 > 1400 µM and a selectivity index > 2.85. Annexin V-FITC/PI analysis showed increased apoptotic populations, with total apoptosis significantly increased at 800 µM. Colony formation analysis further indicated reduced clonogenic capacity. At 400 µM, umbelliferone significantly increased relative Caspase-3/7 and Caspase-9 activities to 1.873 ± 0.635 and 2.483 ± 0.092, respectively, whereas neither activity was significantly increased at 800 µM. In silico ADME analysis predicted properties compatible with commonly used drug-likeness criteria. Conclusions: Collectively, the findings demonstrate effects of umbelliferone on cell viability, apoptosis, clonogenic capacity, and caspase activity in MCF-7 cells, with comparatively lower cytotoxicity toward normal fibroblasts. Computational findings remain hypothesis-generating and do not establish direct target engagement or pathway inhibition. Further mechanistic and in vivo studies are required to determine the biological and pharmacological relevance of these findings.Keywords: umbelliferone, MCF-7, breast cancer, apoptosis, caspase activity, molecular docking, molecular dynamics, ADME

candidates.title: Cardiolipin-Specific Targeting of Melittin via Arg22 in Lipid Membranes: A Natural Toxin-Based Strategy for Treating Mitochondrial Dysfunction in Aging and Disease
candidates.authors: Abaza S, Zhou J, Wang Z, Pan Z, Ma H, Sun Y, Dagda R, Gasanoff E.
candidates.abstract: AbstractBee venom melittin is a small protein with significant pharmacological potential. In this study, AutoDock simulations identified Arg22 as a key residue of melittin responsible for targeting the phosphate groups of cardiolipin (CL). Recombinant melittin with the native amino acid sequence, as well as a modified version with Arg22 substituted by Gly22, were cloned, expressed, and purified. The effects of both melittins on proton adsorption in CL-containing membranes, mitochondrial ATP production, and the formation of non-bilayer lipid structures were examined. Based on the array of computational and experimental data obtained in this work, together with published findings, we propose that Arg22, in tandem with Lys23, targets and neutralizes CL bound to conserved Lys7 and Lys43 of the ATP synthase rotor, thereby detaching CL from the rotor. These events promote a conical shape of CL, which triggers the formation of inverted micelles that entrap protons from the Fo subunit and transfer them to the proton pump of a respiratory complex. This study advances both the conceptual framework of mitochondrial energetics and the translational application of natural toxins. Specifically, the findings support the development of new pharmaceuticals aimed at counteracting the loss of mitochondrial energy production that occurs with aging and pathological conditions.Keywords: melittin, cardiolipin, membrane-mediated proton adsorption, non-bilayer lipid structures, mitochondrial ATP-synthase

candidates.title: Chemical Profiling, Antifungal and Insecticidal Activities of Santolina chamaecyparissus L. Essential Oil: An Integrated Experimental and In Silico Study
candidates.authors: Zouhri A, El-Mernissi R, Houiat A, Abdelfattah B, Khibech O, El-Mernissi Y, Bouhrim M, Basilua J, Zouirech O, S. Alharbi M, A. Mothana R, Al-Yousef H, Senhaji N, Hajji L.
candidates.abstract: Santolina chamaecyparissus L. essential oil (EO) was investigated for its chemical composition, antifungal and insecticidal activities, together with complementary molecular docking and ADMET analyses. GC–MS revealed a monoterpene-rich profile dominated by santolina triene (48.44%), α-pinene (14.05%), camphor (8.80%), myrcene (5.17%), and α-thujene (4.26%). The EO exhibited antifungal activity against Fusarium oxysporum and Aspergillus brasiliensis, with MIC and MFC values of 4 mg/mL and concentration-dependent inhibition of mycelial growth. Insecticidal activity against Rhyzopertha dominica was demonstrated through fumigant, topical-contact, and treated-grain assays, with efficacy varying according to concentration and exposure duration. Molecular docking identified α-thujene and p-cymene as the highest-ranked tested EO constituents against fungal CYP51B and insect AChE, respectively. ADMET predictions highlighted favorable physicochemical characteristics alongside potential toxicity-related liabilities requiring experimental verification. These findings provide a basis for further investigation of S. chamaecyparissus EO and its constituents as potential natural antifungal and insecticidal agents.

candidates.title: Clinical and Genetic Characterization of a Family with Tooth Agenesis Carrying a Novel LEF1 Variant
candidates.authors: Fortuna L, Bertozzi R, Trevisan V, Leoni C, Minucci A, Genuardi M, Isola G, Grippaudo C, Tabolacci E.
candidates.abstract: AbstractBackground: Tooth agenesis is one of the most common developmental anomalies of the human dentition and may occur either as an isolated trait or as part of a syndromic condition. Advances in genomic technologies have facilitated the identification of genes involved in odontogenesis, including LEF1 (Lymphoid Enhancer-Binding Factor 1), a key transcription factor in the WNT signaling pathway. Methods: Whole exome sequencing (WES) was performed in a proband with non-syndromic tooth agenesis to investigate the underlying genetic cause. Parental segregation analysis was performed through Sanger sequencing, and in silico prediction tools were used to assess the potential clinical relevance of the identified variant. A review of the current literature on LEF1-associated dental phenotypes was also conducted. Results: WES identified a novel heterozygous LEF1 variant, c.903G>C, p.(Lys301Asn). The variant co-segregated with the phenotype, being detected in the affected father and absent in the unaffected mother. Although the available evidence is currently insufficient to establish pathogenicity, computational predictions and the known biological role of LEF1 in odontogenesis support its potential functional significance. Conclusions: This study reports a novel LEF1 variant identified in a family with familial non-syndromic tooth agenesis and highlights the importance of integrating genomic findings with clinical and segregation data to inform variant interpretation in hereditary dental anomalies. Further functional and independent genetic evidence will be required to establish the clinical significance of this variant.Keywords: tooth agenesis, LEF1 gene, whole exome sequencing

candidates.title: Comparative Conformational Sampling of Apo Adenylate Kinase by Enhanced Molecular Dynamics and a Sequence-Based Generative Ensemble Model
candidates.authors: Zhao Q, Cui T, Li Y.
candidates.abstract: AbstractConformational sampling remains a major challenge in molecular dynamics (MD) simulations of proteins with large-scale functional motions. Here, we use apo Escherichia coli adenylate kinase (AdK) as a benchmark for the open–closed transition and compare nine sampling protocols under a uniform explicit-solvent budget of 300 ns per method. The methods include unbiased MD, metadynamics, targeted MD (TMD), accelerated MD, simulated tempering, interpolation-based MD, and BioEmu. Closed-state sampling was evaluated relative to a reference-closed basin defined from ligand-stripped PDB 1AKE. TMD was the only method that both reached and maintained the closed reference, whereas unbiased MD did not enter this basin within 300 ns. Metadynamics increased sampling along the domain-distance coordinate but also promoted excessive LID opening, while simulated tempering showed a similar tendency. BioEmu generated closed-like conformations, but these states were not maintained during subsequent short MD simulations. Overall, the results show that collective-variable coverage does not necessarily correspond to stable target state occupancy and that different sampling methods provide different types of conformational information. These findings highlight the importance of selecting sampling strategies according to the specific scientific objective.Keywords: conformational sampling, adenylate kinase, metadynamics, targeted MD, Gaussian accelerated MD, simulated tempering, BioEmu, molecular dynamics, open–closed transition

candidates.title: Comparative In Vitro and In Silico Biological Evaluation of o-Phenylenediamine Conjugates Based on Isofunctional-Surfaced Polyanhydride and Citric Acid-Derived Carbon Quantum Nanodots
candidates.authors: Tunç T, Karakuş G, Çakmak I.
candidates.abstract: This study aimed to comparatively evaluate the anticancer and antimicrobial activities of conjugates formed from poly(maleic anhydride-co-vinyl acetate) (MAVA) and carbon quantum dots (CNDs) with o-phenylenediamine (o-PDA). o-PDA was chosen as the conjugation agent due to its status as a significant aromatic six-membered diamine, which enables specific reactions in the field of drug discovery. MAVA and CNDs, which are low-toxicity carrier systems, were prepared according to a previously developed protocol and conjugated with o-PDA to yield MAVA/o-PDA and CNDs/o-PDA. The structural characteristics of the conjugates were confirmed by ATR-FTIR and 1H-NMR analyses. The cytotoxic effects of the obtained conjugates on MG-63, A549, and MCF-7 cancer cell lines and healthy WI-38 cells, as well as their antimicrobial activities against various Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria, were evaluated. Additionally, ADMET properties and drug-likeness profiles were analyzed in silico to support the biological findings. While neither conjugate induced significant cytotoxicity in healthy WI-38 cells, they exhibited a stronger cytotoxic effect in cancer cells compared to o-PDA alone and the carrier systems. CNDs/o-PDA was found to be more effective than MAVA/o-PDA in MG-63, A549, and MCF-7 cells, whereas MAVA/o-PDA exhibited stronger activity in C6 cells. The conjugates also exhibited higher antimicrobial activity than their individual components, particularly against Gram-negative bacteria. In general, it has been observed that conjugation with o-PDA can enhance the biological activities of MAVA and CNDs while limiting toxicity in normal cells.

candidates.title: Comparative Network Pharmacology and Molecular Docking Analysis of Ursodeoxycholic Acid and Tauroursodeoxycholic Acid in Alzheimer’s Disease-Associated Molecular Networks
candidates.abstract: Background/Objectives: Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is a multifactorial neurodegenerative disorder characterized by amyloid- and tau-related pathology, neuroinflammation, metabolic dysregulation, and neuronal loss. Previous studies have shown the potential effects of bile acids, especially ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) and tauroursodeoxycholic acid (TUDCA), on neurodegenerative diseases. However, whether UDCA and TUDCA exhibit distinct molecular interaction patterns within an Alzheimer’s disease-associated biological context remains unclear. This study aims to compare the relevant targets, enrichment pathways, and docking profiles predicted by UDCA and TUDCA using the computer network pharmacology framework. Methods: The study combined analysis of networks relating to drug action with methods examining how structures bind. We predicted potential targets of UDCA and TUDCA by using public databases and intersected with AD-related genes. Protein–protein interaction network construction, Gene Ontology and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes enrichment analyses, and integrated compound–target–pathway network analysis were performed. Key targets were further evaluated by molecular docking to characterize predicted binding patterns and ligand–target interaction profiles. Results: UDCA and TUDCA share 98 and 103 intersecting genes with AD, respectively, with significant overlapping targets. Functional enrichment analysis showed that UDCA-related targets were significantly enriched in nuclear receptor activity, transcriptional regulation, and metabolic pathways. TUDCA-related targets are more significantly enriched in cell survival, kinase activity and neural activity ligand–receptor interactions. Molecular docking analyses provided target-specific structural information, while same-target docking using GPBAR1 and MAPK14 further revealed ligand-dependent differences in predicted interaction patterns under identical receptor conditions. Results from approaches examining systems and structure both indicate that ursodeoxycholic acid and tauroursodeoxycholic acid show profiles of action that work together. UDCA was associated with predicted upstream regulatory and metabolic-related target profiles, whereas TUDCA showed greater association with intracellular signaling, apoptosis-related, and neuronal survival-related pathways. Conclusions: The two bile acids showed predicted associations with pathways related to cell death regulation, inflammation, and metabolism. These findings provide a methodological basis and testable hypotheses for future experimental validation, but they should not be interpreted as direct evidence of therapeutic efficacy in Alzheimer’s disease.

candidates.title: Computational Analysis of the Homologous Mouse Double RINGs Interface for Targeted Anticancer Drug Design †
candidates.authors: Adewumi A, Sekele L, Oluyemi W, Eze S, Mosebi S.
candidates.abstract: AbstractBackground/Objectives: The new yearly 1.1 million cancer cases and considerably increasing mortality, after decades of decline, require urgent and effective therapy. Targeted anticancer therapy is an attractive strategy for treating cancer by targeting critical receptors. The MDM2-MDMX RING heterodimer downregulates the p53 tumor suppressor pathway, making its disruption a primary therapeutic strategy in oncology. This study evaluates a series of novel inhibitors against the MDM2-MDMX RING interface to identify potent candidates that overcome the binding affinity and structural stability limitations of current small-molecule options like HLI373. Methods: Comprehensive computational simulations and MM/PBSA energy calculations were performed on five inhibitor complexes: Hinokiflavone, MMRi62, MMRi64, MMRi71, and HLI373. Structural stability, flexibility, and compactness were rigorously analyzed across a 200 ns molecular dynamics simulation trajectory using Root Mean Square Deviation (RMSD) and Root Mean Square Fluctuation (RMSF) metrics alongside Principal Component Analysis. Results: Among the evaluated MDM2-MDMX dual inhibitors, MMRi62 demonstrated the strongest binding affinity with a ΔGbind of −26.42 kcal/mol, outperforming reference HLI373 (−14.09 kcal/mol), Hinokiflavone (−22.69 kcal/mol), and MMRi64 (−16.73 kcal/mol). Structurally, MMRi64-bound complexes exhibited the highest stability, achieving the lowest RMSD of 2.28 Å and RMSF of 1.30 Å. Conversely, HLI373-bound complexes displayed pronounced structural fluctuations, yielding a high RMSD of 5.11 Å. Conclusions: These inhibitors present highly promising alternatives to HLI373 for targeting the MDM2-MDMX RING interface. MMRi62 and Hinokiflavone, in particular, stand out as highly potent dual-inhibitor leads for future targeted anticancer therapy development.Keywords: cancer surge, target-based anticancer design, MDM2-MDMX RING protein, dynamic structural conformation, binding mechanism, promising inhibitors

candidates.title: Computational Assessment of CKP-25 Binding at Receptor-Recognition Interfaces Across Diverse Human Coronaviruses
candidates.authors: Papadopoulos A, Petrakis S, Alvarez F, Daras P.
candidates.abstract: AbstractBackground/Objectives: The continued emergence of novel coronaviruses motivates the search for small molecules that bind conserved features of the spike receptor-recognition interface across diverse species. CKP-25 was recently reported as a small-molecule inhibitor of the SARS-CoV-2 spike receptor-binding domain. This study aimed to assess computationally whether CKP-25 can maintain stable binding at receptor-recognition interfaces across phylogenetically diverse human coronaviruses. Methods: CKP-25 was docked to the spike receptor-binding regions of Middle East respiratory syndrome coronavirus (MERS-CoV), severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 1 (SARS-CoV-1), and human coronaviruses NL63, 229E, and HKU1 (HCoV-NL63, HCoV-229E, and HCoV-HKU1). SARS-CoV-2 (PDB 6M0J), for which CKP-25 has documented antiviral activity, was processed identically and included as an experimentally validated reference system. Each selected complex was subjected to three independent 100 ns all-atom molecular dynamics (MD) simulations initialized with different random velocities. Binding stability was evaluated using protein and ligand root-mean-square deviation (RMSD), residue flexibility, radius of gyration, protein–ligand contact persistence, polar interactions, and Molecular Mechanics–Generalized Born Surface Area (MM-GBSA) calculations. Results: CKP-25 was retained at the targeted receptor-recognition interface in all three replicates for four of the five test targets—MERS-CoV, HCoV-NL63, SARS-CoV-1, and HCoV-HKU1—each of which reproducibly engaged the same aromatic and hydrophobic anchor residues in every independent run. HCoV-229E was the sole exception, the ligand relocating from its docked site in two of three replicates. Ligand RMSD plateaus were generally low, mostly below 2.0 Å. Contact analyses indicated a shared dependence on shape-complementary van der Waals packing involving hydrophobic and aromatic residues, including tyrosine- and tryptophan-rich anchoring environments. MM-GBSA estimates, averaged across replicates, ranged from −24.28 to −34.57 kcal/mol. No test target differed from the SARS-CoV-2 reference (−29.15±3.46 kcal/mol) by more than the replicate-to-replicate spread, with MERS-CoV and HCoV-NL63 giving the most favorable means. Conclusions: CKP-25 remained at the receptor-recognition interface of four of the five human coronaviruses tested, and it did so in all three replicates. In the SARS-CoV-2 control, the same pipeline independently reproduced the experimentally established binding mode, which supports the reliability of these predictions. HCoV-229E was the exception: the ligand left the docked site in two of the three replicates, and no contact was reproducible across all three repetitions. Experimental binding measurements and cell-based entry assays are required to test these predictions.Keywords: coronavirus, CKP-25, molecular docking, molecular dynamics, receptor-binding interface, MM-GBSA, in silico binding assessment

candidates.title: Computational Identification of GABA-A Receptor Ligands Targeting the Histamine Allosteric Pocket
candidates.authors: Mihai D, Cornet C, Ion G, Nitulescu G, Olaru O, Zanfirescu A, Kara M, Öztaş E, Nitulescu G.
candidates.abstract: The γ-aminobutyric acid type A (GABA-A) receptor is a key regulator of inhibitory neurotransmission in the central nervous system, and a promising target for cognitive and neurological disorders. Histamine interacts with a distinct allosteric pocket located at the β3–β3 subunit interface, providing an opportunity for the discovery of novel ligands. In the present study, an integrated in silico workflow combining ligand-based similarity analysis, ADMET filtering, molecular docking, and molecular dynamics simulations was applied to identify candidate ligands for this histamine-associated site. Docking analysis showed that ligand efficiency-related metrics discriminated active from inactive ligands more effectively than docking score alone, supporting their use during virtual screening. Three compounds were evaluated by 100 ns molecular dynamics simulations, which showed preserved receptor structural integrity and stable protein–ligand complexes. CHEMBL3236582 exhibited the most favorable dynamic profile, combining low backbone and ligand RMSD (root mean square deviation) values with the most favorable Molecular Mechanics/Poisson–Boltzmann Surface Area (MM/PBSA) binding energy estimate, whereas CHEMBL521996 maintained stable binding despite adopting an alternative binding orientation. Overall, the integrated computational workflow identified CHEMBL3236582 as the most promising candidate for experimental validation and supports further investigation of the histamine-associated allosteric pocket for the discovery of novel GABA-A receptor ligands.

candidates.title: Computational Studies of the Dynamics of the Human Iron Exporter Ferroportin and Insight into the Role of Crucial Residues Involved in Pathogenic Mutations
candidates.authors: Vulterini S, Bonaccorsi di Patti M, Musci G, Polticelli F.
candidates.abstract: AbstractFerroportin (FPN/SLC40A1), the only known human iron exporter, plays a key role in iron homeostasis through an alternating access mechanism involving inward–open, occluded, and outward–open conformations. Pathogenic FPN mutations cause ferroportin–related iron overload, an autosomal dominant iron overload disease characterized by early–onset anemia, hepatic fibrosis, and diabetes. This disease can be further categorized into two subtypes: ferroportin disease, characterized by low transferrin saturation (TSAT) and iron overload predominantly in Kupffer cells, and ferroportin–related hemochromatosis, defined by high TSAT and iron overload in hepatocytes. However, the structural and functional characteristics governing FPN’s conformational transitions and their relationship to pathogenic mutations remain poorly understood. Therefore, we conducted comprehensive modeling and molecular dynamics studies to investigate the conformational states of the transporter and analyze the molecular basis of disease–causing mutations. Our analysis revealed shared dynamic properties across FPN conformations, with all the three main conformations displaying stable protein cores surrounded by dynamic peripheral regions. We observed significant differences in the most stable interactions established between the two lobes of the transporter across the three conformational states, enabling identification of key residues involved in state–dependent stabilization. These findings were interpreted in the context of known pathogenic mutations to assess their potential effects on protein stability and transport mechanism. This approach provides crucial insights into the molecular determinants of FPN function and dysfunction, offering a foundation for understanding how specific mutations disrupt its specific conformational states and lead to ferroportin–related iron overload. The identification of conformationally important residues enhances our understanding of FPN’s transport mechanism and provides a framework for interpreting the pathological consequences of genetic variants in iron metabolism disorders.Keywords: hemochromatosis, ferroportin, iron, molecular dynamics

candidates.title: Computationally Guided Design and Experimental Validation of ssDNA Aptamers Targeting the SARS-CoV-2 Spike Protein
candidates.authors: Márquez Montesinos J, Bernardez A, Mazola Y, Vaccaro L, Sáez-Álvarez Y, Agudo R, Valdivieso E, Llorens-Berzosa S, Fenoy S, González W, Izquierdo F, Ollero D, del Aguila C, Hurtado-Marcos C.
candidates.abstract: Aptamer development has traditionally relied on iterative, labor-intensive experimental approaches. Recent advances in bioinformatics and computational power now enable the rational in silico design of high-affinity nucleic acid ligands, drastically reducing time and cost. Here, we present an integrated computational pipeline for designing ssDNA aptamers targeting the receptor-binding domain (RBD) of the SARS-CoV-2 Spike (S) protein. A library of 4000 randomly generated 20-nucleotide sequences with defined base ratios (C:G:A:T = 3:3:2:2) was screened based on secondary structure and free energy. The 100 most stable sequences (ΔG ≤ −4.1 kcal/mol) were modeled in three dimensions, yielding 1000 conformations. The 100 structures with the lowest potential energies (≤−78,051.7 kcal/mol) were selected for molecular docking with the RBD in the closed, open, and transitional states. Two aptamers—model-2-seq_2714 (seq_2714) and model-5-seq_1397 (seq_1397)—were selected for experimental assessment based on their favorable predicted docking scores against the RBD. Western blot and dot blot assays showed detectable recognition of the recombinant RBD by both aptamers under the experimental conditions tested. Exploratory testing in a limited number of clinical and environmental samples further showed that detectable signals could be obtained in selected complex matrices. These findings provide an initial proof-of-principle assessment of a computational-first strategy for prioritizing candidate aptamers for subsequent experimental testing.

candidates.title: Data Mining Sheds Light on a Novel Family of Plant-Associated Negative-Sense RNA Viruses Linked to Lispiviruses
candidates.authors: Bejerman N, Huebert D, Alvarez-Quinto R, Quito-Avila D, Debat H.
candidates.abstract: Large-scale mining of public transcriptomic datasets can reveal viral diversity that remains invisible to conventional virus-surveillance approaches, while increasingly powerful structure-prediction methods provide a complementary route to characterizing highly divergent viral proteins. Here, we combine sequence detection, phylogenetic analysis, structural prediction, and host-association analyses to investigate the cryptic diversity and biology of a new clade of plant-associated lispi-like viruses. Analyses of RNA-sequencing datasets identified and enabled assembly of 87 coding-complete lispi-like virus genome sequences associated with 75 plant hosts, expanding the known diversity of this new group by approximately 40-fold. The viruses share a conserved four-cistron genome organization, 3′-N(P1)-P2-P3-L(P4)-5′, in which the first cistron is referred to interchangeably as N or P1 and the fourth as L or P4. Structural analyses generate testable structural hypotheses for the four conserved proteins. N (P1) adopts a canonical negative-strand RNA virus nucleocapsid architecture with conserved RNA-interacting residues and a predicted RNA-packaging configuration. P2 is exceptionally divergent, although a subset of structures resembles the ITPase/HAM1 fold. P3 forms a conserved trimeric coiled-coil architecture reminiscent of a viral fusion-protein stalk, but lacks the family-wide sequence features expected of a canonical membrane glycoprotein. L (P4) contains a structurally resolved Mononegavirales-type RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) core with invariant catalytic motifs, including the characteristic GDN signature, whereas its accessory regions are substantially more divergent. Phylogenetic insights form a distinct monophyletic lineage sister to the predominantly invertebrate-associated Lispiviridae, supporting their recognition as the new proposed family Masuviridae, comprising 15 tentative genera. Genus-level clustering is accompanied by marked differences in host association, ranging from strong specialization to broader host ranges. Retrospective screening of public sequencing libraries further identified lispi-like virus sequences in 1536 libraries representing 134 plant species, 11 plant families and 182 geographic locations, highlighting a substantial and geographically widespread cryptic virome. Together, these results establish Masuviridae as a deeply divergent lineage of plant-associated negative-sense RNA viruses and illustrate how the integration of sequence, structural, and large-scale transcriptomic analyses can move viral dark matter from detection towards evolutionary and functional characterization.

candidates.title: Database Mining Reveals Distinct Clusters of Putative Diphthamide-Specific Mono-ADP-Ribosylating Toxins in Vibrio and Aeromonas
candidates.authors: Jørs M, Masuyer G, Jørgensen R.
candidates.abstract: Diphthamide-specific mono-ADP-ribosylating toxins form a structurally conserved but phylogenetically diverse family of AB-type bacterial toxins, with Pseudomonas exotoxin A (PE) serving as a prototypical member. Here, we expand the known diversity of PE-like toxins (PLTs) through comprehensive genome mining and phylogenetic, structural and sequence analyses of PE, Chx, and their Aeromonas and Vibrio cholerae homologues. Aeromonas toxins separate into two distinct groups: a PE-like cluster (AEI) and a cholix-like cluster (AEII), while a fourth cholix subgroup (ChxIV) is identified within V. cholerae, expanding the previously described ChxI–III classification. Although all newly identified toxins retain the core catalytic architecture and hallmark residues essential for ADP-ribosylation of eEF2, they differ in key functional motifs, including receptor-binding residues, furin cleavage loops, and C-terminal ER-retrieval signals, suggesting variation in host-cell uptake routes and intracellular trafficking. Signal peptides were present in all toxins but varied modestly between clusters, consistent with normal species-level Sec-pathway variation rather than divergent secretion mechanisms. Together, our findings provide a significantly expanded overview of PLT diversity and indicate that Aeromonas-derived toxins comprise at least two evolutionarily and mechanistically distinct groups. These insights offer a framework for future functional studies and highlight PLTs as emerging virulence factors in environmentally and clinically relevant bacteria.

candidates.title: Design, Synthesis, and Antifungal Structure‐Activity Relationship of Hydrazide Derivatives Containing a Cyclopropyl Group Against Phytopathogenic Fungi
candidates.authors: Yang S, Wang X, Yin B, Yan W, Wang L, Sha Y, Wang L, Liu Z.
candidates.abstract: ABSTRACTTo discover novel antifungal agents with unique scaffolds for crop protection, a series of 23 hydrazide derivatives containing a cyclopropyl group, including 14 new chemical entities, were designed, synthesized, and evaluated for their antifungal activity against eight phytopathogenic fungi. The in vitro bioassay results at 50 µg/mL revealed that most target compounds exhibited moderate to excellent antifungal activities. Notably, three compounds (4, 6, 7) displayed the most potent broad‐spectrum activity with inhibition rates of 95.0%–100.0% against all eight tested fungi. Their EC50 values were below 10 µg/mL against most fungi. SEM analysis revealed that the parent compound 1 caused pronounced morphological alterations in A. alternata mycelia, including shrinkage, collapse, and irregular distortion, providing a preliminary indication of the cellular effect of the series. Molecular docking of compound 1 with succinate dehydrogenase (SDH) generated a plausible binding model, suggesting SDH as a potential target candidate for this series, pending direct enzymatic validation. SAR analysis demonstrated that the phenyl ring was consistently associated with high activity, and para‐substitution with halogen atoms is favorable for enhancing antifungal activity. These findings suggest that cyclopropyl‐containing hydrazide derivatives, particularly compounds 4, 6, and 7, represent promising lead candidates for the development of novel antifungal agents.

candidates.abstract: To develop human carbonic anhydrase (hCA) IX/XII-targeted therapeutics for glioblastoma multiforme (GBM), novel dithiocarbamate (DTC)-based compounds were synthesized and evaluated for their inhibitory activity against hCA I, II, IX, and XII isoforms. The most potent hCA IX/XII inhibitors were further investigated for their cytotoxic activity against U87 and T98 glioblastoma cells, selectivity toward healthy neuronal cells, and their effects on oxidative stress, inflammatory mediators, and cell death-related pathways. Compounds 4, 9, and 30 emerged as the most promising candidates, with compounds 9 and 30 exhibiting potent cytotoxic activity against both U87 and T98 cells. These compounds acted as dual hCA IX/XII inhibitors with a clear preference for hCA XII. Compounds 9 and 30 modulated the oxidative stress–inflammation axis through regulation of cellular redox balance, and inflammation-associated mediator profiles, including IL-1β, IL-10, TNF-α, and TGF-β. Compound 4 also attenuated oxidative stress and inflammatory signaling in U87 cells. Molecular docking studies supported the experimental findings by revealing favorable binding interactions within the active sites of hCA IX and XII, providing a structural basis for their inhibitory activities. Collectively, these findings identify compounds 4, 9, and 30 as promising DTC-based compounds for GBM therapy through the combined modulation of tumor-associated CAs, oxidative stress, inflammatory, and cell death-related pathways.

candidates.title: Design, Synthesis, and Evaluation of Novel Adenine-Based Hydrazones as Potential Anticancer Agents: Cytotoxicity Against A549 and MRC-5 Cell Lines with In Silico Insights
candidates.authors: Menteşe E, Çalışkan N, Emirik M, Güner A.
candidates.abstract: Background/Objectives: Lung cancer remains a leading cause of global cancer-related mortality, necessitating the development of new therapeutic candidates. In this study, we aimed to design, synthesize, and biologically evaluate novel adenine-based hydrazone derivatives as potential anticancer candidates. Methods: A series of novel adenine–hydrazones were synthesized via the condensation of 2-(6-amino-9H-purin-9-yl)acetohydrazide with various aldehydes and isatin derivatives. Their antiproliferative activities against human lung adenocarcinoma (A549) and normal lung fibroblast (MRC-5) cell lines were evaluated using the MTT assay. Mechanistic investigations—including cell membrane damage (LDH release), oxidative stress (TOS, iROS), mitochondrial membrane potential (MMP, ΔΨm), cell cycle distribution, and apoptosis (Annexin V/PI)—were conducted for the lead derivatives, complemented by multi-target in silico molecular docking against PLK1, TrxR1, and MDM2. Results: Compounds 3d, 3c, and 4j showed the strongest antiproliferative activity within the synthesized series against A549 cells, with IC50 values of 37.2 ± 1.8 µM, 41.8 ± 1.9 µM, and 42.9 ± 1.7 µM, respectively, together with comparatively more favorable A549/MRC-5 activity profiles than several other derivatives. These compounds induced oxidative stress-associated cellular injury, accompanied by mitochondrial depolarization, G2/M phase accumulation, and Annexin V-confirmed apoptotic cell death. Complementary multi-target in silico molecular docking provided theoretical insights into potential binding interactions with PLK1, TrxR1, and MDM2. Conclusions: Adenine–hydrazone hybrids, particularly 5-halogenated isatin derivatives such as compound 3d, provide preliminary lead scaffolds with moderate in vitro cytotoxicity against lung cancer cells, serving as a platform for future structural optimization to enhance potency and selectivity.

candidates.title: Development of P^N-Pd(II) Type Complexes Derived from Aliphatic Amines as Potential Antibacterial and Antifungal Agents
candidates.authors: Acosta-Encinas M, Amaya-Flórez A, Galindo J, Hernández-Ortega S, Alvarez-Ainza M, Juarez J, Orjuela A, Alí-Torres J, Aragón-Muriel A, Reyes-Márquez V, Morales-Morales D.
candidates.abstract: Background/Objectives: The development of new metallodrugs has represented an important milestone in recent years for their potential application in different therapeutic approaches. Therefore, the objective of this study was to synthesize a series of P^N iminophosphine Pd(II) complexes (1Pd–3Pd) incorporating different aliphatic amines. Methods: All complexes were characterized using several spectroscopic and analytical techniques, including 1H, 13C{1H}, and 31P{1H} NMR spectroscopy, mass spectrometry, FT-IR spectroscopy, and elemental analysis. In addition, complex 3Pd was unambiguously characterized by single-crystal X-ray diffraction. Results: Supramolecular studies allowed the main noncovalent interactions responsible for stabilizing the crystal lattice of complex 3Pd to be identified. These interactions were analyzed using Hirshfeld surface analysis, which revealed that C-H···π and C-H···Cl interactions contributed most significantly to the stabilization of the crystal lattice. All complexes exhibited stability in different solvents and positive lipophilicity values, with complex 3Pd displaying the highest hydrophobicity. Through in vitro studies, the minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs) and minimum fungicidal concentrations (MFCs) of all complexes were determined against different Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacterial strains, as well as fungal strains of Candida species. Complex 3Pd exhibited the highest activity, particularly against L. monocytogenes (1.17 µg/mL), P. aeruginosa (4.68 µg/mL), and all fungal strains (18.75 µg/mL), displaying both bactericidal and fungicidal activity. Furthermore, in silico studies enabled the identification of the potential modes of action of the complexes against different molecular targets present in the bacterial and fungal strains. Conclusions: These results demonstrate the efficacy of the three synthesized complexes against different virulent strains exhibiting resistance to broad-spectrum drugs. Furthermore, the presence of the metal center, together with the incorporation of increasingly longer aliphatic chains, appears to enhance the antibacterial and antifungal activity of the complexes.

candidates.authors: Eroğlu M, Mişe Yonar S, Tanrıkulu D, Uslu H, Yonar M.
candidates.abstract: Simple SummaryFish farmers use potassium permanganate to control parasites and harmful microorganisms, but repeated treatments can also affect fish health. In this study, we asked whether curcumin, a natural compound found in turmeric, could help reduce these unwanted effects in common carp. Fish were fed diets containing different amounts of curcumin for eight weeks before exposure to potassium permanganate. Repeated exposure affected their blood and immune responses and weakened their natural defenses against tissue damage. Fish given curcumin showed improvements in many of these measurements. Benefits were observed at 1% of the diet, the lowest amount tested, while 4% offered additional improvements in some measurements. Because smaller amounts were not tested, we could not determine the lowest amount needed for protection. Curcumin may therefore help reduce the physical toll of repeated potassium permanganate exposure. However, we did not assess whether it changes the treatment’s ability to control parasites or bacteria. Further work is needed to establish this and determine whether lower, more affordable amounts offer similar benefits before curcumin can be recommended for this purpose on fish farms.

candidates.title: Diphenylpyraline Derivatives Are Allosteric Agonists of the CB1 Cannabinoid Receptor
candidates.authors: Eldeeb K, Harp J, Fitzgerald R, Leone-Kabler S, Reeves T, Jones S, Childers S, Howlett A, Pulgar V.
candidates.abstract: AbstractDiphenylpyraline analogs JKH1 and JKH10 are monoamine transporter inhibitors and promote relaxation in mouse mesenteric arteries. Here, we evaluated JKH1 and JKH for their interaction with CB1 cannabinoid receptor signaling. In N18TG2 mouse neuroblastoma cells that endogenously express CB1 receptors, JKH1 and JKH10 stimulated [35S]GTPγS binding in a concentration-dependent manner; this stimulation was non-competitively antagonized by the CB1 antagonist-inverse agonist SR141716 (1 µM). JKH10 (but not JKH1) inhibited forskolin-stimulated cAMP accumulation with efficacy as high as the full orthosteric agonist WIN55212-2, and this Gi-mediated inhibition was completely precluded by pertussis toxin treatment. However, JKH1 was a poor inhibitor. The SR141716 failed to completely block the inhibition by JKH10. Both JKH analogs stimulated ERK phosphorylation, but inhibition by SR141716 (1 µM) did not appear to be overcome by increasing concentrations of JKH1 or JKH10. In mouse isolated mesenteric arteries, both analogs (1 µM) attenuated the contractile response, but only the response to JKH10 was blocked by the CB1 antagonist-inverse agonist O-2050 (1 µM). Docking studies to protein data bank CB1 structures 7FEE and 6KQI showed JKH1 was predicted to dock predominantly at a pregnenolone-binding site, whereas JKH10 was predicted to dock at both the pregnenolone and a cholesterol consensus motif at helices 2–3–4 inner membrane leaflet. Thus, a series of diphenylpyraline derivatives can behave as CB1 receptor stimulators, and in silico evidence supports that this could result from interaction with cholesterol and/or pregnenolone protein surface binding sites rather than the orthosteric binding site.Keywords: adenylyl cyclase, biased agonists, cholesterol consensus motif (CCM), diphenylmethoxypiperidine, diphenylpyraline (DPP), extracellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK), G protein-coupled receptors (GPCR), mesenteric resistance arteries, pregnenolone, SR141716, WIN55212-2

candidates.title: Effects of Sanghuang Extract on Candida albicans Colonization and Intestinal Inflammation in a DSS-Induced Colitis Mouse Model
candidates.abstract: Sanghuangporus sanghuang (Sanghuang) extract, obtained from the medicinal and edible fungus Sanghuang, was examined for its inhibitory effects against Candida albicans and its potential role in mitigating intestinal inflammation related to ulcerative colitis (UC). Its anti-Candida albicans activity was assessed by measuring the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC), evaluating its ability to suppress biofilm formation, and observing fungal morphological changes using scanning electron microscopy (SEM). Using mice with dextran sulfate sodium (DSS)-induced UC and intestinal Candida albicans (C. albicans) colonization, fungal burden, intestinal inflammation, mucosal injury, intestinal bacterial community composition, and related signaling pathways were assessed. Sanghuang extract inhibited C. albicans growth and suppressed biofilm formation. SEM further revealed reduced hyphal development and disruption of cell surface morphology following treatment. In vivo, Sanghuang administration ameliorated UC-related phenotypes, with descriptive decreasing trends in fecal C. albicans burden, less severe colonic injury, and lower colonic levels of IL-6, IL-1β, and TNF-α, accompanied by changes in intestinal bacterial community composition. Network pharmacology analysis suggested that pathways associated with phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K)/protein kinase B (AKT) may participate in this process. Molecular docking yielded predicted interactions of caffeic acid with PTGS2, EGFR, PIK3CA, AKT1, and mTOR. qRT-PCR further showed that Sanghuang extract reduced the colonic mRNA expression of Pik3ca, Akt1, and Mtor. These findings provide experimental evidence that Sanghuang extract exerts antifungal activity in vitro and is associated with changes in fecal C. albicans burden and colitis-associated inflammatory responses in this mouse model.

candidates.title: Effects of a Benzimidazolium Salt on Colorectal Cancer Cells: Involvement of Apoptosis and Autophagy
candidates.authors: Cakir M, Acikgoz E, Kuzu B, Akar S, Ozkol H, Donmez-Altuntas H, Akkoc S.
candidates.abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) remains a leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide, necessitating the identification of novel small molecules capable of targeting multiple survival pathways. In this study, the antiproliferative potential of dds benzimidazole-palladium (Pd) complexes was evaluated across breast cancer (4T1, MDA-MB-231) and CRC (DLD-1, HT-29) cell lines using MTT assays. Following initial screening, CRC models were prioritized for mechanistic investigation due to the complexes’ superior cytotoxic profile, particularly that of the lead candidate 3a, which exhibited significant dose-dependent efficacy. Mechanistic analyses, employing immunofluorescence staining for LC3 and mTOR alongside Annexin V/PI flow cytometry, revealed that compound 3a triggers a potent dual response characterized by concomitant autophagy and apoptosis. Furthermore, functional assays indicated that 3a significantly impairs the metastatic hallmarks of CRC cells by inhibiting migration, cell adhesion, and colony formation. Gene expression profiling further elucidated that the anticancer efficacy of 3a is mediated by suppression of the AKT/mTOR/STAT3 signaling axis, thereby triggering an autophagic response that destabilizes cell adhesion and accelerates apoptosis. These molecular findings were corroborated by in silico molecular docking analyses, which demonstrated favorable binding affinities between compound 3a and key regulatory proteins, specifically BCL-2 and Caspase-3. Collectively, these results identify compound 3a as a promising multi-targeted anticancer agent that disrupts critical survival and metastatic pathways in CRC, warranting further preclinical and mechanistic exploration for therapeutic development.

candidates.title: Enhanced Antioxidant and ACE-Inhibitory Activities of L-Theanine Following Formation of the Amadori Compound N-(1-Deoxy-D-Fructose-1-yl)-L-Theanine (Fru-The)
candidates.authors: Li F, Zhou J, Zhang M, Zhang G, Sun W, Ge H, Zhou R.
candidates.abstract: Many amino acids, after undergoing the Maillard reaction with reducing sugars to form Amadori compounds, exhibit significantly enhanced functional activity. In this study, the Amadori compounds derived from theanine, N-(1-deoxy-D-fructose-1-yl)-L-theanine (Fru-The), were synthesized by vacuum dehydration method. The structure of Fru-The was characterized along with the evaluation of its antioxidant and Angiotensin-Converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitory activities. The Fru-The was identified by liquid chromatography tandem mass spectrometry. Its major mass spectrometric fragments were [M+H]+, [M+H-nH2O]+ and [AA+H]+, among others, which are consistent with those of many Amadori compounds previously verified by our team. And our study demonstrated that Fru-The exhibits greater antioxidant properties (ABTS, FRAP, HRSA) and is significantly superior to theanine. Further studies on ACE inhibition have shown that the IC50 value of Fru-Th was 1.400 ± 0.207 mM, whereas theanine showed no obvious ACE inhibition within the tested concentration range up to 10 mM, indicating that Fru-The possesses enhanced ACE inhibitory activities compared to theanine. Fluorescence spectroscopy revealed that the inhibition-related characteristics of ACE by Fru-The may involve both dynamic and static quenching, and the negative ΔG values indicate that the ACE-Fru-The binding process is thermodynamically favorable under the experimental conditions. Specifically, this binding process is endothermic and entropy-increasing (ΔH > 0, ΔS > 0, and ΔG < 0), and it appeared to be more favorable at 37 °C. Molecular docking and circular dichroism spectroscopy further demonstrated that Fru-The binds stably to ACE and significantly alters its higher-order structure. Fru-The exhibits markedly enhanced functional activities compared to theanine and suggest that Fru-The may be a promising candidate for the development of functional tea products.

candidates.title: Evolution-Informed Viroinformatics Identifies Conserved Immune Targets with Predicted Lower Mutational Vulnerability Across Betacoronaviruses
candidates.authors: Alshammari J, Alqahtani H, Alonaizan R, Rahman I, Alzhrani K, Al-Hoshani N, Alwaili M, Aziz T.
candidates.abstract: The extensive evolutionary diversity and continuous mutational adaptation of betacoronaviruses represent a major challenge to the development of broadly protective countermeasures. This study applied an evolution-informed Viroinformatics framework to systematically identify conserved and immune targets with predicted lower mutational vulnerability across betacoronaviruses. The workflow integrated comparative sequence conservation and phylogenetic analysis with immunoinformatics-based epitope screening, HLA population coverage, mutational escape profiling, structural modeling, molecular docking, and molecular dynamics simulations. Conserved cytotoxic T-lymphocyte and helper T-lymphocyte epitopes were prioritized based on immunogenicity, antigenicity, safety, HLA binding potential, evolutionary conservation, and predicted resistance to mutational escape. Combined MHC class I and II analysis predicted a theoretical global population coverage of 99.92%, which requires experimental validation. The resulting 409-amino-acid multiepitope construct was predicted to be antigenic, non-allergenic, and physiochemically stable. Structural validation showed that 99.7% of the residues were located within favored or additionally allowed regions. Molecular docking demonstrated favorable interaction of the vaccine construct with TLR7, while a 100 ns molecular dynamics simulation supported persistence of the predicted vaccine-receptor association. Overall, these findings provide a computational framework for prioritizing evolutionarily conserved immune targets and developing pre-emptive candidate epitopes showing predicted cross-betacoronavirus conservation within the analyzed dataset. Experimental studies evaluating HLA binding, cellular and humoral immunogenicity, recombinant expression, cross-reactivity, and in vivo protection are required to validate the predicted immunological potential and determine whether the proposed construct can provide broad protection against diverse betacoronaviruses.
