candidates.title: From Design to Synergy: Triazine–Triazole Hybrids as Anti-Breast Cancer Leads Targeting Survival and Invasion Pathways for Augmenting Lapatinib Efficacy
candidates.authors: Ali O, Abbas S, Shehat M, Helmy M, Aly M, Teleb M, Khattab S, Abdel-Aziz M.
candidates.abstract: AbstractBackground/Objectives: Breast cancer is the most common cancer diagnosed and the leading cause of cancer-related deaths among women, ranking fourth overall in both sexes. Its treatment is difficult due to drug resistance and side effects from conventional therapies. Developing multitargeted agents and combination approaches offer a promising way to overcome these challenges. This study details the design and testing of new triazole–triazine hybrids as potential anti-breast cancer drugs, exploring their use in combination with lapatinib to enhance its efficacy in breast cancer. Methods: Sixteen triazine–triazole hybrid compounds with amide and ureido linkers were synthesized via click and coupling protocols and tested for their cytotoxic effects on MCF-7 cells using an MTT assay. The most effective compound was evaluated for its inhibitory effect against AXL using an ADP-Glo™ kinase assay, then examined in combination with lapatinib on cellular and molecular levels. In vitro experiments included chemoinvasion assays for metastasis, flow-cytometric analysis of apoptosis, and ELISA to evaluate the molecular mechanisms of promising hits. Molecular docking studies were conducted to simulate the potential target–hit interactions and predict the plausible structural determinants of activity, paving the way for further lead optimization. Results: Compound 6e demonstrated the highest activity (IC50 = 24.58 μM) and good selectivity (SI = 7.87). The combination therapy showed a synergistic effect and increased tumor sensitivity to lapatinib. Biological tests indicated inhibition of the AXL enzyme, downregulation of key pathways (AKT, NF-κB, STAT3, ERK), decreased levels of VEGF, MMP9, and cyclin D1, and increased caspase-3 activity, suggesting apoptosis, which was strengthened by the flow-cytometric analysis findings. Docking results supported multitarget interactions. Conclusions: Compound 6e is a promising multitarget anti-breast cancer candidate with synergistic potential in combination with lapatinib, warranting further in vivo studies.Keywords: AXL inhibitors; lapatinib; 1,3,5-triazines; 1,2,3-triazoles; click reactions; isocyanate synthesis; MCF-7; synergistic combination; molecular docking

candidates.title: Functional Characterization of Uracil-DNA Glycosylase from Staphylococcus aureus
candidates.authors: Koreneva A, Sugirova A, Yakupov B, Safonkina M, Endutkin A, Zharkov D, Saparbaev M, Abeldenov S, Turgimbayeva A.
candidates.abstract: Background/Objectives: Uracil-DNA glycosylase (UNG) initiates base excision repair by removing uracil from DNA. Although Family 1 UNGs are well characterized in model organisms, the biochemical and functional properties of Staphylococcus aureus UNG (SaUNG) is not well characterized. This study aimed to characterize SaUNG. Methods: Recombinant wild-type and mutant SaUNG proteins were examined using biochemical and kinetic assays, site-directed mutagenesis, genetic complementation in Escherichia coli, and in vitro reconstitution of S. aureus base excision repair. Results: SaUNG exhibited maximal activity at pH 8.0–8.5, 37–45 °C, and 100–150 mM KCl and lacked AP-lyase activity. Catalytic efficiencies (kcat/Km) were 1.39 × 109, 3.79 × 108, and 2.93 × 108 M−1·min−1 for ssU, U:G, and U:A, respectively, establishing the preference ssU > U:G > U:A. H180A retained residual activity, whereas simultaneous substitution of Asp59 and His180 abolished detectable activity. Complete inhibition confirmed conserved biochemical properties of Family 1 UNGs. SaUNG complemented the mutation avoidance defect of an E. coli (ung− mug−) mutant and initiated uracil repair in a reconstituted S. aureus base excision repair system. Conclusions: SaUNG is a canonical Family 1 UNG with experimentally characterized biochemical properties, catalytic determinants, and biological function in uracil repair.

candidates.title: Glucose Modulation of the Local Conformational Flexibility and Free-Energy Basin Shape of Human and Yeast Hexokinases: A Comparative Molecular Dynamics Analysis
candidates.authors: Alvarado Y, Méndez A, González-Paz L, Marrero-Ponce Y, Martinez-Rios F, Vera-Villalobos J, Delgado A, Paz J.
candidates.abstract: Simple SummaryCancer cells consume unusually large amounts of sugar to fuel their rapid growth. An enzyme called hexokinase controls the very first step in which cells process this sugar, and in many tumours one of its forms is produced in excess. For this reason, scientists are trying to design drugs that block this enzyme. Because human hexokinases are large and difficult to study, researchers often use the simpler, closely related enzymes from baker’s yeast as stand-ins in computer simulations. We used computer simulations to watch how the human and yeast enzymes move and change shape when sugar binds. Repeating every simulation three times, we found indications that sugar makes the human enzymes more flexible—their overall shape tends to fluctuate more widely—whereas the yeast enzymes barely change or become slightly stiffer: the two organisms appear to respond differently, even though the enzymes look similar and share the same basic function. This suggests that yeast enzymes may not be reliable substitutes for their human counterparts when searching for new cancer drugs on the computer. Such studies may therefore be better when based on the human enzymes themselves, which could help make the search for effective cancer treatments more accurate.

candidates.title: Grb2 phosphorylation antagonizes EGFR-driven ras activation by interfering with condensate assembly
candidates.authors: Phan H, Lin C, Stinger B, DeGrandchamp J, Lew L, Huang S, Groves J.
candidates.abstract: Upon ligand binding, the kinase domain of EGFR phosphorylates multiple tyrosine residues on the receptor cytoplasmic tail through a trans-autophosphorylation process. Phosphotyrosine sites on activated receptors recruit Grb2, which further recruits SOS to initiate downstream signaling by activating Ras. Multivalent binding between SOS and Grb2, as well as direct Grb2:Grb2 interactions, contribute to formation of a protein condensate of activated EGFR. The condensed state of EGFR facilitates autoinhibition release in SOS and exerts regulatory control over signal propagation from activated EGFR to Ras. While kinase activity of EGFR is an essential driver of this signaling process, phosphorylation at residue Y160 on Grb2 blocks Grb2:Grb2 binding and can interfere with EGFR condensation. Here, using a reconstituted system, we examine how titrating kinase activity in the EGFR system can both promote and inhibit signal output to Ras. The results reveal how effects of tyrosine kinase inhibition can, under some circumstances, promote Ras activation by inhibiting negative feedback through Grb2 phosphorylation and disruption of a Grb2 SH2/SH3 dimer interface.

candidates.title: High Conservation of the Human Metapneumovirus Fusion Protein in Contemporary Global Sequences Supports Its Continued Relevance for Therapeutic and Prophylactic Consideration
candidates.authors: Gopalakrishnan V, Schaefer E, Patterson J, Brady T, Francica J, Kushnir A, Podlaha O, Streicher K, Cohen T, Aksyuk A, Tuffy K.
candidates.abstract: AbstractHuman metapneumovirus (hMPV) is associated with severe disease in young children, older adults, and medically high-risk individuals. The hMPV F protein is highly immunogenic and a well-established target of neutralizing antibodies. In-depth hMPV surveillance data remain limited and may provide valuable insight into therapeutic development. Here we assembled a contemporary dataset of F gene sequences acquired from hMPV-positive nasal swab specimens collected between 2022 and 2023, together with contemporary F gene sequences from public surveillance databases, collected between 2017 and 2025. All sequences were subtyped and evaluated for residue-level similarity to reference alleles. Of 724 sequences in the combined contemporary dataset, A2 was the most predominant subtype accounting for nearly half of all sequences (50.83%). The mean F gene sequence similarity to reference alleles was 99.90%, 99.95%, and 99.84% for A2, B1, and B2, respectively; the least conserved residues were the stalk residue 518 for A2 (88.52% similarity to reference allele); BinD residue 450 for B1 (96.60% similarity); and site III residue 36 for B2 (77.88% similarity). Structural analysis showed that observed mutations were predominantly surface-exposed, with no evidence of novel N-linked glycosylation sequons, and were not predicted to significantly alter F protein structure. Overall, these findings indicate that the F protein is highly conserved across subtypes, with sequence variation unlikely to result in meaningful structural differences, thereby supporting development of F-targeted therapeutics against hMPV infection.Keywords: human metapneumovirus, molecular surveillance, viral sequencing, fusion protein, gene sequencing, structural modelling

candidates.title: Huperzine A Attenuates Oxidative Stress-Induced H9c2 Cardiomyoblast Injury Through AKT-Associated Survival Signaling
candidates.authors: Zhang Y, Long H, Qiao L, Zhang H, Chen D, Chen J, Wei B, Li W, Zhou H.
candidates.abstract: Oxidative stress is a major contributor to cardiomyoblast injury and cardiovascular disease progression. Huperzine A (HupA), a natural Lycopodium alkaloid, exhibits antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties, but its cardioprotective mechanisms remain unclear. This study aimed to investigate the effects of HupA on oxidative stress-induced H9c2 cardiomyoblast injury and elucidate the underlying molecular mechanisms. Network pharmacology, molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulations, and cellular thermal shift assay (CETSA) were integrated to predict and investigate AKT1 involvement. An in vitro model of tert-butyl hydroperoxide (tBHP)-induced injury in H9c2 rat cardiomyoblasts was established. Oxidative stress status, mitochondrial function, and AKT-associated signaling were evaluated. The involvement of AKT signaling was examined using MK-2206. HupA significantly improved cell viability in a dose-dependent manner and markedly reduced lipid peroxidation and intracellular and mitochondrial ROS accumulation. In addition, HupA restored antioxidant defenses by increasing superoxide dismutase activity and glutathione levels. Mitochondrial dysfunction induced by tBHP was effectively alleviated, as evidenced by preserved mitochondrial membrane potential and reduced mitochondrial superoxide production. Furthermore, HupA enhanced AKT phosphorylation and MCL-1 expression while inhibiting extracellular HMGB1 release. Importantly, pharmacological inhibition of AKT largely abolished these protective effects, including antioxidant restoration, mitochondrial preservation, and anti-cell death activity. HupA protects H9c2 cardiomyoblasts against oxidative injury through AKT-associated survival signaling, thereby attenuating oxidative stress and preserving mitochondrial integrity. These findings suggest HupA as a promising therapeutic candidate in H9c2 cardiomyoblasts under oxidative stress conditions.

candidates.title: Identification of Novel Potential Tubulin-Targeting Heterocyclic Compounds via Integrated Virtual Screening and In Vitro Studies
candidates.authors: Deyak Y, Khylyuk D, Dudchak R, Finiuk N, Ivasechko I, Kozak Y, Solodiak N, Derkach H, Pietruszyńska M, Podolak M, Gornowicz A, Bielawski K, Bielawska A, Holota S, Lesyk R.
candidates.abstract: AbstractBackground: The development of novel tubulin-targeting agents remains a promising strategy in anticancer drug design. In the present study, novel heterocyclic tubulin-targeting compounds were identified using a complex in silico/in vitro workflow. Methods: An in-house library of approximately 8000 structurally diverse heterocyclic compounds was screened for antiproliferative activity, yielding 260 experimentally validated hits. These compounds were docked against the colchicine, vinca, and taxane binding sites of tubulin. Selected compounds were also tested for their effects on cellular β-tubulin protein levels in Jurkat cells. Results: Docking analysis indicated that 42 compounds matched or exceeded colchicine’s binding energy, 3 compounds were comparable to vinblastine, and 18 compounds surpassed paclitaxel, suggesting the colchicine and taxane sites as preferred targets. Five top-scoring compounds (Les-6370, Les-4272, Les-4309, Les-4403, and Les-1419) were further analyzed via molecular dynamics simulations, confirming stable binding—particularly at the colchicine site—and favorable hydrogen-bonding and lipophilic interactions. At 10 µM, Les-1419 and Les-4309 reduced total cellular β-tubulin protein levels in Jurkat cells by 57.73% and 54.31%, respectively, relative to the effect observed for the reference compound Combretastatin A-4. Conclusions: This study resulted in the identification of novel starting scaffolds with favorable tubulin interaction activity and predicted drug-like properties, representing structurally novel parent structures and serving as promising starting points for further structural optimization and analogue development.Keywords: tubulin inhibitors, molecular docking, molecular dynamics, diarylpyrazoline, heterocyclic compounds, anticancer agents

candidates.title: Identification of Urokinase Plasminogen Activator Receptor (uPAR)-Binding Peptides Using Phage Display: Strategy and Downstream Validation
candidates.authors: Sloth A, Dawoodi I, Treiberg T, Sinkjaer A, Andersen I, Andersen A, Bøgestad E, Rossing M, Stavnsbjerg C, Bakhshinejad B, Kjaer A.
candidates.abstract: Simple SummaryPeptides binding specifically to receptors on the surface of cancer cells can be used for molecular imaging and targeted treatments. However, identifying peptides that bind to the intended target remains challenging because commonly used methods also select false-positive candidates. In this study, we sought to identify peptides with potential binding to the urokinase plasminogen activator receptor, a protein found at high levels in several cancers, and developed an improved biopanning strategy to reduce, although not eliminate, the risk of identifying target-unrelated peptides. Our approach combines peptide phage display with next-generation sequencing, additional selection controls, and several laboratory validation methods to improve the identification of genuine binding peptides. Using this strategy, we selected three candidate peptides for further evaluation of their behavior toward the urokinase plasminogen activator receptor. Our work provides a practical framework for discovering and validating new targeting peptides and may support the future development of more specific imaging agents and targeted therapies.Keywords: biopanning, cancer, next-generation sequencing, peptide, phage display, urokinase plasminogen activator receptor, molecular imaging

candidates.title: Improved cryo-EM reconstruction of sub-50 kDa complexes using 2D template matching
candidates.authors: Zhang K, Grant T, Grigorieff N.
candidates.abstract: AbstractVisualizing the structures of small proteins and complexes has been a longstanding challenge in single-particle cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM). Some of these targets have been successfully resolved by binding to antibody fragments (Fabs) or fusing with external scaffolds to increase their size. Recent advances in conventional single-particle techniques have enabled the determination of an increasing number of structures smaller than 100 kDa, achieving resolutions relevant to drug research. Compared to X-ray crystallography, cryo-EM preserves the near-native states of biomolecules, can resolve structural heterogeneity, and has the potential to apply to a wide range of targets. In this work, we demonstrate that the alignment and reconstruction of small macromolecular complexes can be improved using high-resolution structures as priors, combined with 2D template matching. Using this method, we reconstructed a previously intractable ∼43 kDa protein kinase and improved the density of its ligand-binding site. Our theoretical analysis predicts that this method can further extend single-particle cryo-EM to important drug-binding complexes well below 50 kDa.Research organism: None

candidates.title: In Silico Evaluation of Cyanobacteria-Derived Bioactive Compounds as Potential Monoamine Oxidase-B Inhibitors for Parkinson’s Disease: Molecular Docking and Molecular Dynamics Simulation Study
candidates.authors: Khalid S, Ahmad S, Kaushik A, Sebaei M, Soliman W, Zaidi N, Tripathi R, Nafees S, Rumman M, Yasin D.
candidates.abstract: Background/Objectives: Parkinson’s disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by dopaminergic neuronal loss and impaired motor and non-motor functions. Current therapies provide symptomatic relief but do not prevent disease progression, highlighting the need for novel neuroprotective agents. Cyanobacteria-derived bioactive compounds possess diverse pharmacological properties, including antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activities, making them potential therapeutic candidates. This study aimed to identify potential monoamine oxidase B (MAO-B) targeting cyanobacterial compounds using computational approaches. Methods: Forty-five cyanobacterial bioactive compounds were screened from the literature and databases based on their antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties. Molecular docking against MAO-B was performed using PyRx, and interactions were analyzed using BIOVIA Discovery Studio. The top-ranked compounds were evaluated through ADMET profiling and 100 ns molecular dynamics simulations using the CHARMM36 force field with Swiss-Param-based ligand parameterization. Results: Among the screened compounds, Scytonemin (−11.9 kcal/mol), Calothrixin B (−11.7 kcal/mol), and Zeaxanthin (−11.5 kcal/mol) demonstrated the predicted binding affinity toward MAO-B. ADMET analysis revealed distinct pharmacokinetic profiles among the selected compounds. ADMET analysis showed favorable GI absorption and BBB permeability for Calothrixin B, whereas Scytonemin and Zeaxanthin showed low GI absorption and no predicted BBB permeability. Molecular dynamics simulations indicated stable ligand–protein interactions throughout the simulation period. Conclusions: The integrative computational analysis identified Scytonemin, Calothrixin B, and Zeaxanthin as potential MAO-B-interacting candidates. Based on the combined docking, ADMET, and molecular dynamics profiles, Calothrixin B demonstrated the most favorable overall computational profile, followed by Scytonemin and Zeaxanthin, highlighting all three compounds as candidates for further investigation in MAO-B-targeted drug discovery. Further in vitro and in vivo studies are required to validate their MAO-B inhibitory, neuroprotective, and pharmacokinetic potential.

candidates.title: In Silico Investigation of Candidate Anticancer Targets for Aryltetralin Lignans Previously Reported from Cleistanthus Species
candidates.authors: Nguyen L, Nguyen T, Nguyen D, Mai Q, Le T, Pham-The H, Pham V, Doan T, Tran V, Thai K.
candidates.abstract: AbstractAryltetralin lignans isolated from the fruits of Cleistanthus species exhibit substantial cytotoxic activity, although the molecular interactions underlying these effects remain incompletely understood. This study combined computational target investigation with previously published experimental chemical characterization and cytotoxic evidence and no new isolation or cytotoxicity experiments were carried out. Cleistantoxin, 7-hydroxypicropolygamain, neo-cleistantoxin, cleisindoside A, cleisindoside D, and cleistonkinin D were previously isolated from C. indochinensis, C. tonkinensis, C. eberhardtii and characterized by complementary spectroscopic methods. Cleistantoxin showed potent activity against MCF-7, multidrug-resistant MCF-7R, and HT29 cells, with reported IC50 values of 0.036, 0.014, and 0.035 μM, respectively. Structural similarity to podophyllotoxin-derived anticancer agents guided the investigation of DNA topoisomerase IIβ, Bcl-2, and p53 Y220C as candidate targets. Docking with AutoDock Vina-GPU 2.1 was validated by redocking the co-crystallized inhibitors (RMSD < 2 Å at the TOP2B and Bcl-2 sites; the p53 Y220C control is reported for both receptor preparations), and selected complexes were simulated in triplicate for 100 ns, followed by MM-GBSA calculations and ADMET predictions. Cleisindoside A and D kept etoposide-like hydrogen bonds to DNA in the TOP2B–DNA complex. Their MM-GBSA binding energies were −78.40 ± 3.73 and −81.90 ± 7.84 kcal·mol−1 for two ligand copies, comparable to −79.62 ± 5.14 kcal·mol−1 for etoposide. In Bcl-2, S-10r was clearly more favorable than cleisindoside D. The predicted pharmacokinetic profiles differentiated the aglycones from the glycosides and identified potential cytochrome P450 inhibition liabilities. By linking previously reported experimentally characterized natural products and cytotoxic evidence with molecular modeling, this study provides testable hypotheses for the molecular recognition of Cleistanthus lignans. Direct biochemical and mechanism-focused cellular studies are nevertheless required to validate the proposed targets.Keywords: Cleistanthus, cleistantoxin, aryltetralin lignans, molecular docking, molecular dynamics, MM-GBSA, ADMET

candidates.title: In Silico Structural Dynamics and Downstream Bioprocess of Recombinant Human SUMO-IL-33
candidates.authors: Nguyen K, Mai T, Lam T, Pham L, Do H, Quach M, Thai K, Le M, Nguyen Q.
candidates.abstract: Interleukin-33 (IL-33) is a therapeutic target in inflammatory diseases, yet inhibitor screening is hindered by high commercial protein costs. While expressing IL-33 as a SUMO fusion protein overcomes yield limitations in Escherichia coli, whether this intact chimera can directly serve as a screening surrogate remains unresolved. Here, we combined in silico simulations with empirical bioprocess optimization to establish a high-yield pipeline for native human IL-33 production. AI-based structure predictions (AlphaFold and RoseTTAFold) revealed distinct inter-domain dynamics mediated by a flexible linker. Molecular dynamics simulations of the compact RoseTTAFold model suggested potential steric occlusion near receptor-binding interfaces, whereas AlphaFold models exhibited extended conformations, highlighting model-dependent variations that warrant further structural verification. To restore accessibility, tag cleavage was optimized using 1.0% (mol/mol) SUMO protease at 4 °C for 1 h, achieving near-complete digestion. Sandwich ELISA demonstrated an 87.6% molar epitope recognition recovery for cleaved IL-33 versus only 12.0% for the intact fusion, providing empirical evidence of substantial functional epitope masking by the SUMO tag. Two-step IMAC purification yielded ~19% mass recovery (~32.6% molar recovery). These findings demonstrate that tag removal is operationally essential for IL-33 functional availability in screening applications.

candidates.title: In Vitro Antileishmanial Activity and Cytotoxicity Evaluation of 2-(Thiophen-2-ylmethyl)quinazolin-4(3H)-one Derivatives Against Leishmania tropica and Leishmania infantum
candidates.authors: Karabağ A, Mor B.
candidates.abstract: Background/Objectives: Leishmaniasis is a neglected tropical disease and the toxicity, limited efficacy and emerging drug resistance of current therapies underscore the urgent need for new antileishmanial agents. This study aimed to experimentally assess the in vitro antileishmanial activity, cytotoxicity and selectivity of quinazolin-4(3H)-one derivatives against Leishmania tropica and Leishmania infantum and to computationally investigate the potential interaction of compound E9 with trypanothione reductase. Methods: The in vitro antileishmanial activities of sixteen quinazolin-4(3H)-one derivatives (E1-E16) against the promastigote forms of L. tropica and L. infantum were evaluated. Additionally, the most active compounds were subjected to an evaluation of their cytotoxicity in human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs) and their selectivity indices (SIs) were subsequently calculated. Molecular docking and molecular mechanics/generalized Born surface area (MM/GBSA) analyses were performed for compound E9 against L. infantum trypanothione reductase. Results: Compounds E2, E9 and E11 showed activity against L. tropica, with half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC50) values of 23.2, 22.4 and 76.0 μM, respectively. In contrast, compounds E2, E3, E9 and E11 were active against L. infantum, with IC50 values of 38.1, 69.7, 28.2 and 86.7 μM, respectively, suggesting species-dependent activity. Furthermore, among the tested compounds, E2 showed the most favorable selectivity profile against L. tropica and L. infantum, with SI values of 8.8 and 5.4, respectively. Moreover, molecular docking of E9 produced a docking score of −8.070 kcal/mol, with MM/GBSA analysis indicating a binding free energy of −82.44 kcal/mol. Conclusions: These findings support further investigation of quinazolin-4(3H)-one derivatives as potential antileishmanial agents, with E2 emerging as the most selective compound. Furthermore, they suggest that the biological activity of this compound series may differ among Leishmania species. The molecular modeling findings suggest a potential interaction between E9 and trypanothione reductase, supporting the need for further evaluation of these compounds in intracellular amastigote models and subsequent in vivo studies.

candidates.title: In Vitro Susceptibility and Molecular Docking of Echinocandins Against Clinical Dermatophyte Isolates: Implications for Resistant Dermatophytosis
candidates.authors: Haghani I, Nikjan I, Yahyazadeh Z, Lagzian M, Valadan R, Javidnia J, Shokohi T, Hedayati M, Yazdani J, Nosratabadi M, Vaseghi N, Abastabar M, Badali H.
candidates.abstract: Drug-resistant dermatophytosis has emerged as a global therapeutic challenge, underscoring the need for alternative antifungal strategies. Echinocandins, inhibitors of β-(1,3)-D-glucan synthase, demonstrate potent activity against Candida and Aspergillus but remain insufficiently characterized against dermatophytes. This study evaluated the in vitro activity of anidulafungin and caspofungin in a diverse clinical collection and examined their predicted interactions with β-(1,3)-D-glucan synthase. Antifungal susceptibility testing was performed on 105 clinical isolates, including T. indotineae, T. mentagrophytes, T. rubrum, T. tonsurans, M. canis, N. gypsea, and T. violaceum, using CLSI M38-A3 broth microdilution. Minimum effective concentrations (MECs) for echinocandins and minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs) for comparator agents were determined. Molecular docking simulations were conducted to characterize echinocandin interactions with β-(1,3)-D-glucan synthase. Statistical analyses used Kruskal–Wallis and Dunn’s tests. Both echinocandins showed significantly lower MEC/MIC distributions than all comparator antifungals after adjustment for multiple comparisons (all adjusted p < 0.001). Anidulafungin was more potent than caspofungin (GM MECs: 0.011 vs. 0.022 µg/mL; p < 0.001). Against terbinafine-resistant T. indotineae, MEC50 values were 0.008 µg/mL (anidulafungin) and 0.016 µg/mL (caspofungin), markedly outperforming terbinafine (MIC50 = 4 µg/mL). Docking analyses demonstrated species- and ligand-dependent predicted interaction patterns with β-(1,3)-D-glucan synthase, providing complementary structural context for the observed in vitro susceptibility profiles. This study extends prior in vitro observations by profiling two echinocandins against diverse clinical dermatophytes, including terbinafine-resistant T. indotineae. Docking analysis provides structural context but does not establish target engagement. Further preclinical studies are needed to confirm therapeutic relevance.

candidates.authors: Mardale G, Dumitrașcu V, Pop R, Dumitru C, Muntean D, Mioc M, Mioc A, Mara B, Balan-Porcarasu M, Budu O, Negrea-Ghiulai R, Șoica C.
candidates.abstract: Background/Objectives: One of the major problems facing the medical world is cancer, which causes millions of deaths each year. Nitrogen-containing heterocycles appear to offer a potential solution to this problem. Thus, the present study aimed to synthesize and characterize—both physicochemically and biologically—the new compounds obtained by combining benzotriazole and 1,2,4-triazole scaffolds. Methods: Each of the four cell lines (HaCaT—human keratinocyte, A375—melanoma, A549—non-small cell lung cancer, and HT-29—colorectal adenocarcinoma) was treated for 48 h with concentrations ranging from 10 to 100 µM of the four compounds. After 48 h of treatment, changes in cell viability were assessed using the Alamar Blue assay. These findings were supplemented by microscopic analysis of metabolic changes, as well as alterations in the actin cytoskeleton and nuclei, using staining techniques. Results: The results showed that MG-1 (p-chlorophenyl-) and MG-3 (p-(N,N-dimethylamino)phenyl-) are the most active compounds in our study, with IC50 values for each tumor line as follows: 75.43 ± 2.77, 77.15 ± 1.32, and 96.28 ± 1.72 μM in A375, A549, and HT-29 cells, and 78.97 ± 3.08, 56.78 ± 2.57, and 69.19 ± 3.97 μM, respectively. In HaCaT cells, IC50 values remained above 100 μM for all four hybrids. In silico screening identified MEK1 as the most favorable target for the investigated series, while 100 ns molecular dynamics simulations and MM-GBSA analysis supported stable binding of MG-1 and MG-3, with predicted binding free energies of −54.83 and −40.70 kcal/mol, respectively. Conclusions: Even with a limited set of compounds, we can conclude that the biological effect observed in our study depended on both the cell line and the substituent attached to the aryl moiety. The results obtained for MG-1 and MG-3 suggest that these compounds may serve as suitable starting points for further structural optimization and investigation of the mechanisms of action.

candidates.title: Insights on the effect of extracellular acidification on an HCN channel: A molecular dynamics study
candidates.authors: Asgharpour S, Lazaratos M, Spehr M, Carloni P.
candidates.abstract: AbstractExtracellular acidification can alter the structure and function of ion channels by neutralizing acidic residues exposed to the extracellular space. However, the relationship between protonation states and alterations in the structural dynamics of the channel is difficult to investigate by experiments. Here, we used atomistic simulations and graph-based algorithms to predict the H-bond pattern of the mouse hyperpolarization-activated cyclic nucleotide-gated (HCN2) channel, whose gating is facilitated by extracellular acidification. Our simulations revealed that E212 — a residue exposed to the extracellular space absent in human HCN channels — participates in a complex hydrogen-bond network with the transmembrane domain. These networks are partially disrupted at acidic pH levels, affecting the molecular interactions of the S4 helix in the channel’s voltage-sensing domain. On the basis of our findings, we suggest that hydrogen-bond network alterations under acidic extracellular conditions can affect channel’s gating.

candidates.title: Integrated Network Toxicology, Molecular Dynamics Simulation and In Vitro Assays Identify EGFR, ESR1 and IGF1 as Core Mediators of Bisphenol S-Exacerbated Polycystic Ovary Syndrome
candidates.authors: Liu J, Ye G, Liu X, Deng Z, Ma Y.
candidates.abstract: AbstractBisphenol S (BPS), an environmental endocrine disruptor, has been implicated in polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), but its underlying molecular targets remain largely uncharacterized. Here, this study integrated network toxicology, molecular simulations and in vitro cellular assays to identify key mediators of BPS-associated PCOS. A total of 199 overlapping target genes between BPS exposure and PCOS were screened from public databases, predicted hub genes were extracted via protein–protein interaction (PPI) network construction and 30 core hub genes were enriched in oxidative stress, hormone response, inflammation, cell-cycle regulation, and PI3K-Akt, FoxO, AGE-RAGE, and endocrine resistance pathways by Gene Ontology (GO) and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathway enrichment analysis. Using molecular docking simulations found that the top 15 hub proteins exhibited favorable binding affinities for BPS, with binding free energies below −5.0 kcal/mol. Molecular dynamics simulations revealed that BPS binding induced only minor conformational perturbations in EGFR and ESR1, with negligible effects on backbone stability, core domain flexibility, global compactness and surface properties. In contrast, BPS association effectively dampened global backbone fluctuations and the residue-level mobility of IGF1, and the intermolecular hydrogen bond strength followed the order IGF1 > EGFR > ESR1. In KGN cells, BPS suppressed cell viability and proliferation in a time- and dose-dependent manner while upregulating the protein levels of EGFR, ESR1 and IGF1; notably, IGF1 was most sensitive to low-dose BPS exposure. These findings suggest that BPS may exacerbate PCOS progression by upregulating EGFR, ESR1 and IGF1 to inhibit granulosa cell growth, and thereby disrupt ovarian oxidative homeostasis, hormone signaling, insulin metabolism and cell-cycle regulation via the PI3K-Akt and FoxO pathways. This study provides a theoretical framework for assessing the reproductive health risks of BPS, and lays a foundation for further experimental validation and population-based epidemiological research.Keywords: bisphenol S, polycystic ovary syndrome, network toxicology, molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulation

candidates.abstract: This research aimed to evaluate structural, physicochemical and pharmacokinetic characteristics of racemic 2-hydroxy-3-(4-phenylpiperazin-1-yl)propyl 4-[(alkoxycarbonyl)amino]benzoates (Ib)–(IVb) and 2-hydroxy-3-[4-(R-substituted phenyl)piperazin-1-yl]propyl 4-[(alkoxycarbonyl)amino]benzoates (1b)–(12b), while further extending the in vitro screening of their racemic salts, 1-(3-{4-[(alkoxycarbonyl)amino]benzoyloxy}-2-hydroxypropyl)-4-(R-substituted phenyl)piperazin-1-ium chlorides (I)–(IV) and (1)–(12) (alkoxy = methoxy to butoxy in all of these series, and R = H, 4′-F, 2′-F or 2′-OCH3), against several mycobacterial species, including a slow-growing virulent Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) H37Rv strain. candidates.abstract: Isometamidium chloride (ISM) is a widely used trypanocidal drug for treating animal trypanosomiasis, despite concerns about toxicity, and emerging drug resistance. Owing to the unavailability of a crystal structure for Trypanosoma evansi, the co-crystal structure of the catalytic domain of thymidine kinase from T. brucei (5FUW, 2.20 Å) was used for computational studies. candidates.title: Integrative Multi-Omics and Network Pharmacology Analyses Reveal Potential Mechanisms of Codonopsis pilosula in Mountain Sickness
candidates.authors: Zhou Y, Wu J, Tan Z, He W, Tan W, Fu M, Bai B, Li H.
candidates.abstract: Mountain sickness comprises a spectrum of high-altitude disorders associated with hypobaric hypoxia, including acute mountain sickness (AMS) and high-altitude pulmonary edema (HAPE). Although Codonopsis pilosula has been widely used in traditional medicine for conditions related to hypoxia, its molecular basis in mountain sickness remains poorly understood. Here, we integrated network pharmacology, transcriptomic analysis, machine-learning-based feature selection, single-cell RNA sequencing, and molecular docking to explore potential molecular associations between Codonopsis pilosula-related candidate targets and mountain sickness. We identified a set of Codonopsis pilosula-associated candidate targets enriched in biological processes related to hypoxia response, oxidative stress, inflammation, and vascular regulation. Integrated transcriptomic analyses across high-altitude exposure, AMS, and HAPE revealed convergent alterations in immune-related and oxygen transport-associated programs. Machine-learning analysis further provided internal computational prioritization of candidate genes associated with high-altitude exposure, with recurrent selection across complementary algorithms within the analyzed paired cohort. Single-cell transcriptomic analysis provided additional cellular context for these candidates, revealing distinct expression patterns across peripheral blood and lung cell populations. Molecular docking further identified potential interactions between selected Codonopsis pilosula compounds and candidate proteins, with MMP9, CA2, and BCL2 showing comparatively favorable predicted interactions. Together, these findings provide an exploratory framework for evaluating potential associations between Codonopsis pilosula-associated candidate targets and transcriptional and cellular responses to high-altitude hypoxia, and identify candidate molecular pathways and targets for further experimental investigation.

candidates.title: Investigation of Potential Mechanisms of Yerba Santa Compounds Against Alzheimer’s Disease
candidates.authors: Arevalo Navarro M, Alfano C, Cross J, Zhai T, Shen L, Huang Z.
candidates.abstract: AbstractAlzheimer’s disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder in which chronic neuroinflammation plays a central role in disease initiation and progression. Yerba Santa (Eriodictyon spp.) is a medicinal plant with reported anti-inflammatory and neuroprotective properties, although its molecular mechanisms remain poorly understood. This study investigated whether chemically characterized Yerba Santa compounds show predicted docking interactions with neuroinflammation-related protein targets implicated in AD. Thirty-six ligand structures, representing 30 mass spectrometry peak assignments, were docked against 30 neuroinflammation-related proteins using the MolSoft ICM molecular docking platform. To improve reproducibility, each ligand–target pair was evaluated by replicated docking simulations followed by statistical analysis, with apo and holo targets evaluated against separate statistical references and expanded docking where applicable. Under the apo −25 kcal/mol screening reference, 11 ligand–target pairs were retained after BH-FDR correction and expanded docking for the apo C1r-C1s (PDB:6F39). Separately, 23 holo ligand–target pairs were retained after comparison with their corresponding redocked native-ligand references: Complement C1q (PDB:2JG8), GABA-A receptor α1β2γ2 (PDB:6D6U), and NLRP3 (PDB:7PZC). The pairs retained under these separate criteria involved multiple Yerba Santa compounds, predominantly flavonoids, while Rosmarinic acid (L21) was retained for both Complement C1q (PDB:2JG8) and NLRP3 (PDB:7PZC). These findings support a selective predicted multi-target interaction profile for Yerba Santa compounds and identify complement signaling, GABA-A receptor-associated neurotransmission, and NLRP3 inflammasome signaling as testable pathways for future experimental studies of neuroinflammation in AD.Keywords: Alzheimer’s disease, Yerba Santa, Eriodictyon, molecular docking, statistical validation, neuroinflammation, flavonoids, complement system, natural products

candidates.title: Irreversible Inhibition of Human Ornithine Aminotransferase: A Quantum Mechanics/Molecular Mechanics Study
candidates.authors: Zhang Y, Guan X, Gong A, Wang G, Zhang Q, Li Y, Wang W, Wang Q.
candidates.abstract: Human ornithine aminotransferase (hOAT) is overexpressed in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and participates in glutamine anabolic metabolism, making it a promising therapeutic target. Although (1S,3S)-3-amino-4-(hexafluoropropan-2-ylidenyl)-cyclopentane-1-carboxylic acid (named here as BCF3 after the (bis)trifluoromethyl feature) has been proposed as a potent inhibitor of hOAT, previous experimental studies have characterized an external aldimine intermediate and the static end-state adduct, but the elementary fluorine-elimination steps and their modulation by the active-site environment remain incompletely understood. Herein, molecular dynamics (MD) and quantum mechanics/molecular mechanics (QM/MM) calculations were employed to systematically explore the irreversible inhibitory mechanism mediated by external aldimine II—the key reaction intermediate of BCF3—against hOAT. Conserved active-site water molecules act as proton-shuttling bridges, and residue-dependent electrostatic effects control fluorine elimination. External aldimine II forms a stable covalent adduct with Lys292 and sequentially releases fluorine atoms from the –CF2 moiety via water-mediated Fα− and Fβ− elimination, with feasible barriers of 10.8 and 16.0 kcal/mol, respectively. Negative overall reaction energies indicate that the elimination products are energetically favored in the system. Electrostatic and noncovalent interaction analyses suggest that Arg180 and Gly42 promote fluorine elimination whereas Phe177 suppresses it, providing an atomistic explanation for the superior inhibitory potency of the bis-trifluoromethyl scaffold. The atomistic inhibitory mechanism uncovered in this study provides a theoretical foundation for the future rational design of hOAT-targeted drugs for hepatocellular carcinoma therapy.

candidates.title: K34 (3,3″-Dihydroxy-6′-desmethyl Terphenyllin) Promotes Hemoglobin-Supported H2O2 Decomposition and Attenuates Neurodegenerative Phenotypes in APP/PS1 Mice with Focal GiD
candidates.authors: Park Y, Choi B, Park M, Kim M, Won W, Shin H, Lee C.
candidates.abstract: AbstractHydrogen peroxide (H2O2) contributes to oxidative stress in Alzheimer’s disease (AD), yet conventional antioxidants that directly scavenge H2O2 have shown limited therapeutic efficacy. Here, we investigated K34 (3,3″-dihydroxy-6′-desmethyl terphenyllin), a catechol-bearing para-terphenyl isolated from the marine fungus Penicillium janthinellum 168CLC-17.1, as an indirect H2O2-decomposing agent. Complementary cell-free assays showed that K34 promoted peroxidase-dependent H2O2 decomposition, including Hb-supported H2O2 decomposition, while molecular docking predicted a plausible binding pose near the Hbβ heme pocket. In amyloid-β42 (Aβ42)-stimulated primary astrocytes, K34 reduced intracellular H2O2. In APPswe/PSEN1dE9 (APP/PS1) mice subjected to focal GFAP-inducible diphtheria toxin receptor (fGiD), systemic K34 attenuated memory impairment, preserved NeuN-positive neurons, reduced GFAP immunoreactivity, and improved hippocampal spike probability. K34 also exhibited low passive blood–brain barrier (BBB) permeability and limited inhibition of five major cytochrome P450 (CYP) isoforms under the tested conditions. These findings extend Hb-supported H2O2 decomposition to a structurally distinct marine natural product and support further evaluation of K34 as an antioxidant scaffold for modulating oxidative stress-associated neurodegenerative phenotypes.Keywords: hydrogen peroxide, hemoglobin, pseudoperoxidase, Alzheimer’s disease, oxidative stress, marine natural product

candidates.title: Kaempferol-3-O-Rutinoside (K3R) Promotes Functional Rehabilitation by Modulating S100β and Inflammation Following Induced Traumatic Injury to Sciatic Nerve in Mouse Model
candidates.authors: Iman T, Muzaffar H, Zubair M, Hussain G.
candidates.abstract: AbstractHighlights What are the main findings? K3R improved sensorimotor functional recovery following sciatic nerve crush injury in mice.K3R reduced oxidative stress and proinflammatory cytokine levels and improved muscle fiber morphology after nerve injury. What are the implications of the main findings? K3R shows promising neuroprotective potential by attenuating oxidative and inflammatory responses following peripheral nerve injury.K3R may represent a potential candidate for developing therapeutic strategies to enhance functional recovery after sciatic nerve injury.AbstractBackground: Peripheral nerve injury causes substantial functional impairment and represents a major health concern worldwide. Peripheral nerve injuries are sequelae of iatrogenic injuries, occupational trauma, and motor vehicle crashes. The available therapeutic approaches, including pharmacological treatment, surgical repair, and rehabilitation, are mostly management therapies rather than curative treatments. Consequently, functional recovery is never achieved. There is a dire need for new therapeutic approaches to facilitate functional restoration. Kaempferol-3-O-rutinoside (K3R) is a plant-derived flavonoid glycoside known for its potent anti-inflammatory and antioxidant properties. Flavonoids may promote tissue recovery following injury by modulating inflammatory responses and reducing oxidative stress. However, the effect of K3R on functional recovery following peripheral nerve injury has not yet been investigated. Therefore, this study aimed to evaluate the effects of K3R on early functional recovery following sciatic nerve crush injury in mice. Methods: Twenty-four BALB/c mice were equally allocated to three groups (n = 8): (1) Sham, (2) Ctrl (Control), and (3) K3R treatment group. K3R (2.5 mg/kg) was dissolved in DMSO and administered intraperitoneally once a day from the time of sciatic nerve injury until the conclusion of the experiment. The Ctrl and sham groups received an equal volume of DMSO according to the same dosing schedule. Sensorimotor function recovery was assessed using behavioral tests, including grip strength, pinprick, sciatic functional index (SFI), and hot plate tests. Hematological and biochemical assays were performed to assess total blood count and oxidative stress markers. Muscle fiber morphology was evaluated by morphometric analysis. Proinflammatory cytokines (TNF-α and IL-6) were measured as indicators of the systemic inflammatory response, whereas S100β protein levels were measured as a marker associated with neural injury and glial responses following sciatic nerve injury. Results: K3R treatment significantly enhanced early sensorimotor function recovery compared with the Ctrl group (p < 0.001). Significant differences in oxidative stress markers TAC (p < 0.001), TOS (p < 0.001), MDA (p = 0.003), and CAT (p = 0.007) were observed among the experimental groups. When comparing the K3R-treated group to the Ctrl group, morphometric analysis revealed an increase in the diameter of muscle fibers (p = 0.011). The levels of IL-6 (p = 0.042) and TNF-α (p = 0.005) indicated attenuation of the systemic inflammatory response, while reduced S100β levels (p = 0.002) were observed in the K3R-treated group, consistent with reduced injury-associated changes. Conclusions: Our findings suggest that K3R may facilitate early functional recovery following sciatic nerve injury, potentially by attenuating oxidative stress and systemic inflammatory responses. However, the precise mechanisms underlying this remain to be elucidated. Future studies should therefore focus on identifying the molecular pathways involved in K3R-mediated recovery, as well as axonal regeneration, Schwann cell activity, and remyelination. Long-term investigations incorporating structural, morphometric, and molecular assessments will be essential to understand its regenerative efficacy and translational potential.Keywords: Kaempferol-3-O-rutinoside, sciatic nerve injury, motor functions, sensory functions, oxidative stress, inflammation

candidates.title: LC–MS-Based Metabolomic Profiling of Excoecaria agallocha Leaf Extract: Integrated Antioxidant, Anti-Inflammatory, Cholinesterase Inhibitory and Neuroprotective Evaluation with AChE-Targeted Molecular Docking
candidates.abstract: AbstractExcoecaria agallocha L. is a medicinally important mangrove species containing diverse secondary metabolites with potential antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and neuroprotective activities. This study investigated the multifunctional biological potential of E. agallocha leaves using petroleum ether, chloroform, ethyl acetate, methanol, and aqueous extracts. Preliminary phytochemical screening revealed a solvent-dependent distribution of constituents, while total phenolic and flavonoid contents were quantified in the methanolic and aqueous extracts. Antioxidant activity was evaluated using DPPH radical-scavenging and ferric-reducing antioxidant power (FRAP) assays, while anti-inflammatory activity was assessed using protein-denaturation and COX-2 inhibition assays, with aspirin and celecoxib as reference standards, respectively. Cytotoxicity of the methanolic and aqueous extracts was evaluated in L929 normal fibroblasts, and neuroprotective activity was assessed in SK-N-SH neuroblastoma cells exposed to trimethyltin (TMT), with the aqueous extract administered 1 h before TMT exposure. Apoptotic changes were evaluated using acridine orange/ethidium bromide (AO/EB) dual-fluorescence staining. Acetylcholinesterase (AChE) inhibition was determined using galantamine as the reference inhibitor. LC–MS was employed for putative metabolite profiling of the aqueous extract, followed by AChE-targeted molecular docking of selected identified compounds against human acetylcholinesterase (AChE; PDB ID 7E3D) and ProTox-II-based in silico toxicity prediction. The aqueous extract showed the highest total phenolic (717.81 µg/g) and flavonoid (485.16 µg/g) contents compared with the methanolic extract (562.43 and 334.00 µg/g, respectively) and demonstrated the strongest DPPH radical-scavenging activity among the extracts (IC50 = 115.49 µg/mL) together with a marked ferric-reducing capacity. The aqueous extract also exhibited pronounced COX-2 inhibition (IC50 = 39.77 µg/mL), whereas the methanolic extract showed greater inhibition of protein denaturation (IC50 = 138.89 µg/mL). The aqueous extract displayed relatively low cytotoxicity toward L929 cells and markedly attenuated TMT-induced toxicity in SK-N-SH cells, with the greatest protection observed at the lowest pre-treatment concentration (20 µg/mL; 92.14 ± 1.77% cell viability versus 16.92 ± 1.55% with TMT alone). AChE inhibition by the aqueous extract increased concentration-dependently, with an IC50 of 55.64 µg/mL. Consistent with these findings, AO/EB staining demonstrated an increased proportion of viable cells and reduced apoptotic cell populations following aqueous-extract pre-treatment. LC–MS profiling revealed a chemically diverse array of putatively identified metabolites. AChE-targeted molecular docking putatively identified 6-hydroxy-2-(4-methoxyphenyl)-4H-chromen-4-one and daidzein showed comparatively favorable docking profiles together with Class 5 predicted toxicity. Collectively, the present findings demonstrate that E. agallocha leaf extracts possess measurable antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, cholinesterase-inhibitory, and neuroprotective-related activities under the experimental conditions investigated, with the aqueous extract showing comparatively pronounced activity. These findings provide preliminary experimental and computational evidence supporting further bioassay-guided isolation, experimental validation of individual compounds, mechanistic studies, and in vivo evaluation to determine the neuroprotective potential and biological relevance of E. agallocha.Keywords: Excoecaria agallocha, antioxidant activity, COX-2 inhibition, acetylcholinesterase, neuroprotection, trimethyltin

candidates.title: Machine Learning-Guided Virtual Screening Identifies a Novel MELK-Targeted Antiproliferative Lead Compound with G2/M Arrest Activity in Triple-Negative Breast Cancer and Lung Adenocarcinoma Cells
candidates.authors: Cao W, Jiang B, Chi X, Li W, Yang H, Li X, Zhao Y, Zhang X, Meng R, Cang Y, Du G, Wang J.
candidates.abstract: Simple SummaryMaternal embryonic leucine zipper kinase (MELK) is a promising anticancer target, but the discovery of novel MELK inhibitors remains challenging due to the inefficiency of conventional high-throughput screening approaches. Here, we established an integrated machine learning-guided virtual screening workflow combining hierarchical docking, MM/GBSA rescoring, ADMET prediction, and molecular dynamics simulations to prioritize 12 candidates from approximately 15.58 million compounds. Among three commercially available compounds tested, CPD6 emerged as a structurally novel lead with low-micromolar antiproliferative activity against triple-negative breast cancer (MDA-MB-468) and lung adenocarcinoma (H1299) cells, outperforming the reference inhibitor MELK-8a. Cellular thermal shift assay in cell lysates provided biochemical evidence of MELK engagement, and functional assays demonstrated that CPD6 suppresses colony formation, inhibits DNA synthesis, and induces G2/M arrest via downregulation of the CDC25C-CDK1-Cyclin B1 axis. These findings support CPD6 as a cell-active lead for further optimization and validate the utility of this computational pipeline in anticancer drug discovery.

candidates.title: Metabolic Profiling, Antioxidant Activity, and Mechanistic Insights of Chicory from Northern and Southern China: Integrating Metabolomics, Machine Learning, Molecular Docking, Molecular Dynamics Simulations, and In Vitro Assays
candidates.authors: He D, Li Y, Zhang J, Yang Q, Lian W, Li J, Yang L.
candidates.abstract: Chicory is a traditional food–medicinal plant, and its antioxidant efficacy has been recognized. However, the specific differences in the metabolic characteristics and antioxidant activity of chicory caused by geographical differences remain unclear. In this study, a total of 64 volatile components and 35 non-volatile components of northern and southern chicory were identified. Chemometric combined with machine learning was applied to screen 8 volatile and 7 non-volatile potential chemical biomarkers. Furthermore, the core targets of the chicory antioxidant were revealed by network pharmacology prediction combined with molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulation. The results of in vitro antioxidant assays illuminated that the antioxidant activity of northern chicory was significantly stronger than that of the southern samples (p < 0.01). This study reveals that geographical environments may affect the metabolites and antioxidant activity in chicory by regulating secondary metabolism, and it also provides a scientific basis for the application of chicory as a natural antioxidant in functional foods.

candidates.title: Molecular Characterisation of the Nuclear Localisation Sequence Binding Properties of Toxoplasma gondii Importin α
candidates.authors: Mehta D, Banerjee B, Coulibaly F, Wagstaff KM, Patankar S, Bhaumik P, Jans DA.
candidates.abstract: AbstractThe classical nuclear import pathway in eukaryotic cells is mediated by the importin (IMP) α and β1 heterodimer, where IMPα acts as an adaptor protein that recognises and binds to nuclear localisation signals (NLSs) on nuclear protein cargoes. IMPα from Toxoplasma gondii (TgIMPα), the causative agent of toxoplasmosis, is an essential gene and validated druggable target, but its NLS binding properties remain largely uncharacterised. To investigate the NLS binding properties of purified TgIMPα we designed NLS peptides and compared its properties with those of mammalian (mouse) IMPα by AlphaScreen binding assays. The well-characterised viral NLS from simian virus SV40 large tumour-antigen (T-ag NLS) was recognised by TgIMPα with low-nM binding affinity comparable to Mus musculus IMPα (MmIMPα), whereas a T. gondii-specific NLS from the GCN5 gene product (TgGCN5) exhibited high affinity binding to TgIMPα but not MmIMPα. Mutational analysis of basic residues within the NLSs indicated pronounced binding selectivity. To elucidate the structural basis of these interactions, molecular dynamics (MD) simulations of an ab initio TgIMPα model bound to each NLS was performed. Key polar, salt-bridge, and cation-π interactions driving NLS recognition were identified. Critically, the lysine at position 2 (Lys128 in T-ag and Lys95 in TgGCN5) of each NLS engages conserved threonine and aspartate residues at the major binding site, playing an essential role in binding stability. Strikingly, TgIMPα displayed a more extensive and distinct cation-π interaction network than MmIMPα, revealing that, while the overall NLS binding architecture is conserved, specific pocket variations underlie differential high affinity recognition. Collectively, this study provides insights for the first time into the molecular distinctions in NLS binding between parasite and mammalian IMPα, potentially representing the foundation for future selective targeted drug design or peptidomimetic strategies against T. gondii.Keywords: Toxoplasma gondii, nuclear import, NLS peptides, biophysical assays, MD simulations

candidates.title: Molecular Docking, Metabolite Profile, In Vitro Antioxidant, Anticholinergic, Antidiabetic, and Antiglaucoma Properties of Royal Jelly
candidates.authors: İzol E, Yerebasan Ü, Kayaoğlu E, Turhan M, Yılmaz M, Necip A, Sağlamtaş R, Akıncıoğlu H, Gülçin İ.
candidates.abstract: AbstractBackground/Objectives: Royal jelly is a biologically active bee product with a complex chemical composition and diverse biological properties. This study aimed to comprehensively characterize the phytochemical composition of royal jelly and evaluate its antioxidant capacity, enzyme-inhibitory abilities, and potential molecular interactions with target enzymes. Methods: The phytochemical profile of royal jelly was characterized using liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry (LC–MS/MS). Total phenolic and flavonoid contents were determined spectrophotometrically. Antioxidant activity was evaluated using DPPH•, ABTS•+, and DMPD•+ scavenging assays, together with Fe3+, CUPRAC, and FRAP reducing methods. Enzyme-inhibitory abilities were assessed against human carbonic anhydrase I and II (hCA I and hCA II), acetylcholinesterase (AChE), butyrylcholinesterase (BChE), α-glucosidase, and α-amylase. Molecular docking analyses were subsequently performed to investigate the interactions of major identified compounds with enzyme active sites. Results: LC–MS/MS analysis revealed a diverse profile of phenolic and flavonoids, including quinic acid, caffeic acid, chlorogenic acid, p-coumaric acid, apigenin, luteolin, kaempferol, and amentoflavone. Royal jelly exhibited considerable antioxidant activity, with IC50 values of 29.33, 29.20, and 21.65 μg/mL in the DPPH•, ABTS•+, and DMPD•+ scavenging assays, respectively. It also demonstrated notable reducing capacity in Fe3+ reduction (0.702 μg/mL), CUPRAC (1.444 μg/mL), and FRAP (0.964 μg/mL) assays. Significant inhibitory ability was observed against hCA I (1.12 μg/mL), hCA II (1.33 μg/mL), AChE (1.44 μg/mL), BChE (1.52 μg/mL), α-glucosidase (2.04 μg/mL), and α-amylase (2.11 μg/mL). Docking analyses indicated that major constituents, particularly quinic acid, could interact with key catalytic residues through hydrogen bonding and electrostatic interactions. Conclusions: Royal jelly possesses a rich polyphenolic profile accompanied by substantial antioxidant and multi-target enzyme-inhibitory abilities. These findings provide biochemical and molecular evidence supporting the potential of royal jelly as a functional food and nutraceutical ingredient and highlight its value as a source of bioactive compounds for further pharmacological investigation.Keywords: royal jelly, antioxidant, metabolite profile, enzyme inhibitions, molecular docking

candidates.title: Molecular Interactions of Bioactive Peptides with Proteins and DNA
candidates.abstract: Background: This study investigates the molecular recognition of two biologically active peptides (P1 and P2) by key biomacromolecular targets. The studied peptides were previously identified in Babylon snail hydrolysates and have been shown to exhibit antioxidant and cytotoxic activities against Caco-2 colorectal cancer cells. Given their reported biological potential, we decided to investigate both compounds from a different perspective. Their interactions with human serum albumin (HSA), alpha-1-acid glycoprotein (AAG), lysozyme (LYS), immunoglobulin G (IgG), and DNA were evaluated. Methods, Results and Conclusions: Spectroscopic analyses revealed concentration-dependent binding of the studied peptides to plasma proteins under investigations. Notably, peptide binding did not substantially alter the secondary structure of the target proteins, indicating that complex formation occurs without significant structural perturbation. Molecular docking further supported the formation of peptide–protein complexes, highlighting the contribution of hydrogen bonding and hydrophobic contacts to molecular recognition. The combined spectroscopic and docking results were consistent with a predominantly non-intercalative, possibly minor-groove-associated interaction with ctDNA. Taken together, these findings provide a comparative physicochemical characterization of the interactions of P1 and P2 with selected proteins and ctDNA. These findings provide insight into the molecular recognition properties of P1 and P2 and support further investigation of their biological relevance.

candidates.title: Multi-Target Anti-Aging and Wound-Healing Potential of Libyan Thymus vulgaris and Thymus capitatus Essential Oils: Integrated GC–MS, Network Pharmacology, Molecular Docking, and In Vitro Evaluation
candidates.authors: Suliman S, Al-Masawri A, Hassan M, Abouzeid S.
candidates.abstract: AbstractThymus vulgaris (TV) and Thymus capitatus (TC) are traditionally used for skin-related disorders, but their comparative chemical composition and multi-target skin-protective mechanisms remain insufficiently characterized. In this study, essential oils from aerial parts collected in eastern Libya were analyzed by GC–MS and evaluated using network pharmacology, molecular docking, enzyme-inhibition and antioxidant assays, and a human fibroblast scratch-wound/RT-qPCR model. GC–MS identified 39 constituents, accounting for 98.95% and 99.23% of the TV and TC oils, respectively; carvacrol (41.38%) and thymol (20.91%) predominated in TV, whereas thymol (41.06%) and carvacrol (13.02%) predominated in TC. Chemometric comparison with 28 published oils per species (PCA and hierarchical clustering) classified the TC oil as a thymol chemotype, found in only seven of 28 regional T. capitatus oils (18 were carvacrol type), and the TV oil as a carvacrol-rich type most similar to Moroccan oils. Network pharmacology identified 1074 core targets linked to 14 skin-associated conditions and prioritised 50 hub genes, including NFKB1 and RELA. Docking of 129 compound–target pairs showed that 84 (65%) achieved docking scores ≤−5.0 kcal/mol. TC showed stronger elastase, tyrosinase, hyaluronidase, and 5-LOX inhibition, whereas TV exhibited stronger COX-2 inhibition and antioxidant activity. At a low-toxicity concentration (1.99 µg/mL), TC was associated with accelerated fibroblast wound closure, which may reflect both migration and proliferation, and with increased COL1A1, ITGA11, and HAS2 and decreased MMP1 mRNA expression. Overall, the two oils displayed complementary multi-target anti-aging, anti-inflammatory, and antioxidant activities in vitro and in silico, with TC additionally suggesting pro-regenerative potential in fibroblasts, supporting their further investigation as topical cosmeceutical candidates.Keywords: Thymus vulgaris, Thymus capitatus, essential oil, GC–MS, network pharmacology, molecular docking, skin aging, enzyme inhibition, wound healing, chemotype, chemometrics

candidates.title: Multiscale Computational Prioritization of Chromone-Based Acetylcholinesterase Ligands
candidates.authors: Khibech O, Abdelfattah B, Bouhrim M, Alqahtani M, Alqahtani J, Miantezila Basilua J, Boulouiz A, Touzani R.
candidates.abstract: Identifying acetylcholinesterase (AChE) ligands for Alzheimer’s disease research requires integrating molecular recognition with pharmacokinetic and safety considerations. Here, four designed chromone derivatives (M1–M4) were investigated to determine how conformational sampling and complementary molecular descriptors refine docking-based prioritization. Donepezil redocking in human AChE and cross-docking into Torpedo californica AChE recovered the crystallographic and transferred reference orientations, respectively, with RMSDs of 0.942 and 1.074 Å. Molecular docking was integrated with 800 ns molecular dynamics, MM/PBSA, electronic-structure calculations, and pharmacokinetic/toxicity predictions. M4 achieved the most favorable chromone docking score (−9.6 kcal mol−1), whereas M3 yielded the most favorable chromone MM/PBSA estimate within the 775–800 ns window (−23.90 ± 2.31 kcal mol−1). Donepezil retained a more favorable MM/PBSA estimate (−41.00 ± 2.75 kcal mol−1). M4 exhibited the highest electronic hardness, while predicted toxicity profiles revealed distinct liabilities across the series. The divergence between docking and sampled energetics highlights the value of integrating complementary criteria when selecting compounds for experimental evaluation. These protocol-dependent findings prioritize M3 and M4 as complementary computational candidates requiring experimental confirmation of AChE inhibition, selectivity, and safety.

candidates.title: Multiscale Interactome Analysis Prioritizes Candidate Herbs and Compounds for Diabetic Retinopathy
candidates.authors: Ahn Y, Chae J, Han S, Lee W, Park C.
candidates.abstract: AbstractDiabetic retinopathy (DR), a leading cause of preventable vision loss among working-age adults, arises from chronic hyperglycemic injury to the retinal microvasculature; current interventions such as anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) injection are largely reactive, and mechanism-anchored herbal options remain undefined. We constructed a multiscale interactome and applied a biased random-walk diffusion model to prioritize herbal candidates, candidate compounds, and mechanisms for DR. Herb–ingredient records were drawn from OASIS; ingredient targets from DrugBank, TTD, and STITCH; and disease genes from DisGeNET. For each herb and compound, we computed diffusion profiles, correlated them with the DR profile, and assessed target-overlap significance by hypergeometric test. Eleven herbs combining high correlation (top 5%) with significant overlap (p < 0.05) were retained, led by Pini Koraiensis Semen (0.0263), Benincasae Exocarpium (0.0183), and Veratri Rhizoma Et Radix (0.0162); none had been previously investigated for DR. CASP3 emerged as a target shared by all eleven herbs, and enrichment analysis highlighted the advanced glycation end product–receptor for AGE (AGE–RAGE), TNF, IL-17, and NF-κB pathways alongside apoptosis and reactive-oxygen-species responses. Compound-level analysis recovered evidence-supported quercetin, resveratrol, oleic acid, luteolin, and diosgenin and nominated tectorigenin and cucurbitacins as novel candidates. This framework recapitulates known DR biology and elevates testable multi-target leads that warrant experimental validation for diabetic retinopathy.Keywords: diabetic retinopathy, network pharmacology, multiscale interactome, biased random walk, herbal medicine, candidate compounds

candidates.title: Myricetin Modulates Quorum Sensing-Associated Phenotypes, Virulence, and Biofilm Formation in Pathogenic Bacteria: In Vitro and In Silico Studies
candidates.authors: Bazaid A, Saeedi N, Jalal M, Alkayyal A, Patel M, Aldarhami A.
candidates.abstract: AbstractBackground/Objectives: The rapid emergence of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) among pathogenic bacteria has necessitated the development of alternative therapeutic strategies that target bacterial virulence rather than cell viability. Methods: In this study, the flavonoid myricetin was systematically evaluated for its antibacterial, QS-associated phenotypic and biofilm formation-inhibitory activities against clinically relevant bacterial pathogens. Results: Myricetin exhibited moderate antibacterial activity and significantly reduced several QS-associated phenotypes. Violacein and prodigiosin production were reduced by 74.59% and 64.32%, respectively, consistent with QS-modulatory activity under the tested conditions. Furthermore, myricetin markedly attenuated key virulence factors in Pseudomonas aeruginosa, including pyocyanin (70.44%), pyoverdine (75.84%), and rhamnolipids (48.69%). In addition, concentration-dependent reductions in biofilm formation and extracellular polymeric substance (EPS) production was observed across all tested strains. Molecular docking predicted favourable interactions of myricetin with key QS regulatory proteins, particularly CviR and LasR, which was supported by molecular dynamics simulations. Notably, the LasR–myricetin complex showed greater computational stability among the evaluated complexes, supporting its potential role as a key interaction site. Conclusions: This study provides an integrated experimental and computational evaluation of myricetin-mediated modulation of QS-associated phenotypes across multiple bacterial systems, demonstrating reductions in virulence-factor production and biofilm formation under the tested conditions. Collectively, these findings position myricetin as a promising anti-virulence candidate, although further studies are required to validate its clinical applicability.Keywords: myricetin, QS-associated phenotypes, QS modulation, antimicrobial resistance (AMR), biofilm formation inhibition, anti-virulence strategy

candidates.title: Niosomal Mexiletine Attenuates Rotenone-Induced Parkinsonism via Modulation of the circDLGAP4/miR-134-5p/p-CREB Axis and Restoration of Mitochondrial–Autophagic Homeostasis
candidates.authors: Raafat E, Alanazi F, Alanazi S, Mansour Y, Teiama M, Mohamed S.
candidates.abstract: AbstractBackground: Parkinson’s disease (PD) is distinguished by progressive dopaminergic degeneration driven by the convergence of oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and impaired autophagy. Mexiletine (Mexil), which has demonstrated antioxidant properties, has not been systematically investigated yet for its potential to mitigate mitochondrial-dysfunction-related neurodegeneration in PD. Using an integrated computational and experimental approach, we characterized, for the first time, the neuroprotective mechanisms of Mexil’s action against rotenone (Rot)-induced Parkinsonism and employed niosomes as a nanocarrier platform to enhance mexil delivery and augment its neuroprotective potential in a Parkinson’s disease model. Methods: Molecular docking identified candidate molecular targets underlying niosomal Mexil’s neuroprotective potential. Sprague–Dawley male rats were assigned to control, Rot, and Rot plus niosomal Mexil (30 and 50 mg/kg) groups. Motor performance was evaluated, while dopaminergic degeneration, oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and autophagy were assessed biochemically, histopathologically, and immunohistochemically. Results: Docking revealed promising interactions between Mexil and both phosphorylated cAMP response element-binding protein (p-CREB) and alpha-synuclein, with binding scores of −5.2 and −4.9 kcal/mol, respectively. Niosomal Mexil improved motor function, restored dopamine and tyrosine hydroxylase levels, and curtailed alpha-synuclein accumulation. Most notably, niosomal Mexil engaged a previously unexplored circular RNA DLGAP4/microRNA-134-5p/p-CREB axis, promoted mitochondrial biogenesis via the phosphorylated AMP-activated protein kinase (p-AMPK)/peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator 1-alpha (PGC-1α)/sirtuin-1 (SIRT-1) pathway, and rebalanced mitochondrial dynamics. These changes were accompanied by restored autophagic axis and suppressed oxidative stress and inflammation. Conclusions: Niosomal Mexil confers neuroprotection against Rot-induced Parkinsonism by orchestrating oxidative, mitochondrial, autophagic, and inflammatory pathways, positioning it as a mechanistically novel disease-modifying candidate warranting further preclinical evaluation in PD.Keywords: rotenone, niosomal mexil, mitochondrial dysfunction, circDLGAP4/miR-134/p-CREB, PGC-1α, autophagy

candidates.title: Novel Benzimidazol-2-Acetamide Derivatives as Submicromolar Casein Kinase 1δ Inhibitors with Favourable Predicted Drug-like Properties
candidates.authors: Ceni C, Calenda S, Vagnoni G, Marinari E, Catarzi D, Varano F, Trevisan L, Fornasier M, Federico S, Spalluto G, Novello G, Salmaso V, Moro S, Calamai M, Colotta V.
candidates.abstract: Background/Objective: Casein kinase 1δ (CK1δ) plays a central role in regulating circadian rhythms, DNA repair, apoptosis, and cell proliferation, and its dysregulation is associated with both cancer and neurodegenerative diseases, making CK1δ an attractive therapeutic target. This study aimed to develop novel CK1δ inhibitors with favourable drug-like properties through the synthesis and biological evaluation of benzimidazol-2-acetamide derivatives. Methods: A novel series of benzimidazol-2-acetamide derivatives was synthesized, incorporating different substituents on the benzimidazole core (5-chloro, 5,6-dichloro, 5-nitro, and 5-cyano) and various saturated cyclic amines on the acetamide moiety. Compounds were evaluated for CK1δ inhibitory activity, while molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulations were performed to investigate their binding mode. In silico ADME predictions assessed pharmacokinetic properties, and cytotoxicity was evaluated in SH-SY5Y neuroblastoma cells. Results: The 5,6-dichloro derivatives 20 and 24, bearing piperidin-4-ylmethanamine and morpholine moieties, respectively, displayed the highest CK1δ inhibitory activity (IC50 = 0.172 and 0.223 μM). The 5-cyano analogue 22 also exhibited a good potency (IC50 = 0.224 μM). Computational studies confirmed an ATP-competitive binding mode and highlighted the dynamic behaviour of the solvent-exposed substituents within the CK1δ binding site. Predicted pharmacokinetic properties suggested favourable oral absorption and blood–brain barrier penetration. Compounds 20, 22, and 24 showed no cytotoxicity in SH-SY5Y cells at concentrations up to 10 μM. Conclusions: The new benzimidazol-2-acetamide derivatives exhibited good inhibitor activity against CK1δ, favourable predicted ADME properties, and low cellular toxicity. The combined experimental and computational findings provide valuable insights for the further optimization of this scaffold toward the development of therapeutics for CK1δ-related diseases.

candidates.title: Novel indole derivatives containing a thiosemicarbazide moiety as potential antioxidant agents for fresh beef preservation
candidates.authors: Wang T, Xiao L, Ren Y, Wu M, Liu Y, Tang J, Wan S, Peng J.
candidates.abstract: AbstractOxidative stress is implicated in numerous pathological processes. Developing efficient, safe small-molecule antioxidants is of great medicinal interest. In this work, ten new indole derivatives bearing a thiosemicarbazide moiety (4a–4j) were synthesized and fully characterized by 1H NMR, 13C NMR, and HRMS. In vitro antioxidant assays indicated that all target compounds showed obvious free radical scavenging potency. Among them, compound 2-(3-(1H-indol-3-yl)propanoyl)-N-(4-chlorophenyl)hydrazine-1-carbothioamide (4i) displayed the strongest in vitro ABTS radical scavenging activity with an IC50 = 0.96 μg/mL, remarkably lower than that of vitamin C (1.87 μg/mL). Compound 4i also exhibited excellent in vitro DPPH scavenging efficiency (IC50 = 2.95 μg/mL). Molecular docking and 100 ns molecular dynamics simulations predicted that compound 4i stably bound to the catalytic pocket of human peroxiredoxin 5 (PDB ID: 1HD2). Meanwhile, in silico ADMET and drug-likeness predictions suggested favorable physicochemical properties, acceptable safety, and compliance with Lipinski’s rule of five. Furthermore, application in a raw beef patty model revealed that compound 4i effectively retarded myoglobin oxidation, suppressed pH elevation, and preserved red-color stability during refrigerated storage, exhibiting superior color-protection performance. Collectively, these findings highlight compound 4i as a promising dual-purpose candidate, deserving further investigation both as an antioxidant lead for drug discovery and as a potential protective agent for raw meat preservation, with additional enzyme-level and food-safety assessments required.Keywords: admet, antioxidant agents, drug-likeness, indole, molecular simulation, thiosemicarbazide
